What you'll learn

  • Create a Google Colab notebook that saves to your own Drive.
  • Check that Python, transformers, PyTorch, scikit-learn, NumPy, and matplotlib are present and recent enough.
  • Install or upgrade a library inside Colab, and restart the session so the new version loads.
  • Switch between CPU and GPU runtimes and confirm which one you got.
  • Decide whether you need a Hugging Face account, and store its token as a Colab secret instead of in your code.

Here is a sentence and what a 65-million-parameter model said about it. You'll run this exact model in the next lesson:

By Module 4 you'll be able to explain every number in that output: how the sentence became 17 tokens, how each token got a vector, and how the vectors became the labels PER, LOC, and ORG. First you need a place to run it. That place is Google Colab, and setting it up takes about ten minutes.

#What you need, and what you don't

  • A Google account. A personal account is the safe choice. Some school accounts have Colab switched off by an administrator, and you'll see an access page instead of a notebook.
  • A browser on any computer, Chromebooks included.
  • No GPU and no installs. Colab runs Python on a Google virtual machine. transformers, PyTorch, scikit-learn, NumPy, and matplotlib are already installed there.
  • A Hugging Face account is optional. Every model in this course is public, so you can download them without signing in. The last section explains when an account helps.

This course has two kinds of code. Cells that run on the page (the ones with output underneath) use only scikit-learn, NumPy, and matplotlib on small texts typed into the cell, and the output you see came from actually running them. Cells that download a model from the Hugging Face Hub are marked as Colab cells; run those in your notebook, where the download happens on Google's machine.

#Create your course notebook

  1. Go to colab.research.google.com (opens in a new tab) and sign in at the top right.
  2. Choose File › New notebook in Drive.
  3. Click the name Untitled0.ipynb at the top left and rename it, for example nlp-m1-setup.ipynb.
  4. Click into the empty code cell, type print("hello"), and press Shift+Enter.

The first run takes a few seconds while Colab connects you to a machine, called a runtime. Once it's connected, small RAM and Disk bars appear at the top right and the output shows under the cell. In Google Drive, the notebook is now in a folder named Colab Notebooks.

Windows

Shift+Enter runs a cell and moves to the next. Ctrl+Enter runs it and stays put. Ctrl+M B adds a code cell below. Tools › Keyboard shortcuts lists the rest.

macOS

Shift+Enter runs a cell and moves to the next. Cmd+Enter runs it and stays put. Cmd+M B adds a code cell below. Tools › Keyboard shortcuts lists the rest.

Chromebook

Same as Windows: Shift+Enter runs and moves on, Ctrl+Enter runs and stays, Ctrl+M B adds a cell below. Colab works fully in the Chrome browser, so nothing else is needed.

#Check that every library is there and new enough

Paste this into a new cell and run it. It reads each package's installed version without importing it, so it's quick, and it flags anything missing or too old for this course.

That output is from the machine that built this page. Your Colab will show its own version numbers, probably different ones, and that's fine as long as every line says ok. Notice the comparison uses tuples of integers: (4, 57) >= (4, 40) is true, but comparing the strings "4.100" and "4.40" would give the wrong answer, because text compares character by character.

#Install or upgrade a library, then restart

If a line says MISSING, or a later import stops with an error saying no module has that name, install it in a new cell:

To upgrade a package that's too old, add -U:

Then choose Runtime › Restart session and run the version cell again. People skip the restart and then wonder why nothing changed. Python had already loaded the old package into memory, and new files on disk don't replace a module that's already imported. A restart starts a fresh Python process that imports the new copy.

📝 Note

Installs last only as long as the runtime. When Colab gives you a new machine (after you disconnect, after a long idle stretch, or the next day), the preinstalled versions are back. If you needed an install, keep that %pip cell at the top of the notebook.

#Choose CPU or GPU

Every notebook in this course runs on Colab's free CPU runtime. A GPU only makes the transformer cells faster, and on short sentences you'll barely notice. When you do want one:

  1. Choose Runtime › Change runtime type.
  2. Under Hardware accelerator, pick T4 GPU (the free option), then Save.
  3. Run this check:

On a T4 runtime it prints:

Changing the runtime type gives you a different machine, so all your variables are gone afterwards. Run your setup cells again. Free GPU time has a usage limit that Google doesn't publish and that changes over time; when you hit it, Colab says it can't connect to a GPU backend and offers a CPU runtime instead. Take it: nothing in this course needs the GPU.

#Optional: a Hugging Face account and token

The Hugging Face Hub (opens in a new tab) hosts the models you'll download. Public models need no account. An account helps in two cases: models whose owners require you to accept terms before downloading (these are called gated models), and heavy use, where signed-in downloads get higher rate limits.

If you make one:

  1. Sign up at huggingface.co/join (opens in a new tab), then open Settings › Access Tokens and create a token with Read permission.
  2. In Colab, click the key icon in the left sidebar to open Secrets, choose Add new secret, name it HF_TOKEN, paste the token as its value, and switch on Notebook access.
  3. Restart the session. The Hugging Face libraries find a secret named HF_TOKEN on their own, so your code never contains the token.

Without a token, your first download prints a warning that begins The secret HF_TOKEN does not exist in your Colab secrets and ends by saying authentication is still optional for public models. That warning is harmless. The download carries on.

⚠️ Watch out

Never paste a token into a code cell. Notebooks are easy to share, and anyone with the notebook could use the token as you. If you ever do, delete it on the Access Tokens page and create a new one.

#Optional: the same tools on your own computer

Colab is the supported path, and it's the only one that works on a Chromebook. If you'd like to work offline, install Python 3.10 or newer from python.org (opens in a new tab), then make a virtual environment for the course:

Windows

Open PowerShell in a folder for the course and run:

If PowerShell refuses to run the activate script, run Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned once and try again.

macOS

Open Terminal in a folder for the course and run:

Linux

Open a terminal in a folder for the course and run:

On Linux the default PyTorch download includes GPU libraries and is several gigabytes. The selector at pytorch.org/get-started/locally (opens in a new tab) gives a smaller CPU-only command.

JupyterLab opens in your browser and works like Colab. Run the version check there too.

#Problems people hit on day one

  • "You do not have access" or a blank page when opening Colab. Your school account has Colab disabled. Sign in with a personal Google account.
  • The version cell still shows the old number after %pip install -U. You didn't restart. Choose Runtime › Restart session, then run the cell again.
  • "Cannot connect to GPU backend". You've used up the free GPU allowance for now. Continue on CPU, or try again later.
  • The HF_TOKEN warning on the first download. Harmless for public models. Add the secret if you want it gone.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You run %pip install -U transformers, it finishes without errors, and the version check still prints the old version. What do you do?

  • The new files are already on disk. Installing again changes nothing while the old copy is loaded in memory.

  • Python keeps using the module it already imported until the process restarts.

  • The runtime type has nothing to do with which package version is loaded.

Show answer

B. Python keeps using the module it already imported until the process restarts.

2Where should a Hugging Face token live in a Colab notebook?

  • Anyone you share the notebook with could read it and use your account.

  • The libraries read it from there, and it never appears in the notebook's code or output.

  • Public models download without any token; it's needed only for gated models or higher rate limits.

Show answer

B. The libraries read it from there, and it never appears in the notebook's code or output.

3You change the runtime type from CPU to T4 GPU halfway through a notebook. What happens to the variables you'd created?

  • Colab doesn't move Python state between machines.

  • A new runtime type means a new virtual machine with a fresh Python process.

Show answer

B. A new runtime type means a new virtual machine with a fresh Python process.

Key takeaways

  • Colab runs your notebook on a Google machine with the NLP libraries preinstalled; notebooks save to Colab Notebooks in your Drive.
  • Check versions at the top of a notebook. After %pip install -U, restart the session or the old version stays loaded.
  • The free CPU runtime is enough for this course. A T4 GPU is optional, limited, and comes with a fresh machine.
  • A Hugging Face token is optional. If you have one, keep it in Colab Secrets as HF_TOKEN, never in a cell.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Run a scikit-learn text cell and read its output.
  • Download a tokenizer from the Hugging Face Hub and see how it splits a sentence.
  • Run a named-entity pipeline and print its results in a readable form.
  • Fix the three errors people meet on a first run: a misspelled model name, a missing key, and a download that can't connect.
  • Finish with a check cell that fails loudly if anything is broken.

Your notebook from the last lesson can print version numbers. That proves the libraries exist, not that they work. A setup is only proven when real text goes in and sensible output comes out, so this lesson pushes one sentence through each layer you'll use in the course: scikit-learn first, then a tokenizer, then a full model.

Keep working in the notebook you made in the last lesson, or create a new one called nlp-m1-first-run.ipynb.

#Step 1: Count words with scikit-learn

This cell runs entirely on your machine, with no downloads. It turns three short support messages into a table of word counts, which is the oldest trick in NLP and the starting point for Module 2.

The first line of output is the vocabulary: every distinct word, lowercased and sorted. Each row of the table is one message, and each column counts one vocabulary word. Look at the column for charged: it's 1 in the first and third rows, because both messages contain it. Notice what's missing, too: the single-letter word I and the punctuation. CountVectorizer keeps only tokens of two or more letters or digits unless you tell it otherwise. You'll take that rule apart in Module 2.

If your Colab output matches this, scikit-learn works.

#Step 2: Download a tokenizer from the Hub

Run this in Colab. The first time, it downloads a few small files from the Hugging Face Hub:

"dslim/distilbert-NER" is a model's address on the Hub: the account dslim, then the model name. AutoTokenizer reads the model's config, works out which kind of tokenizer it needs, and loads its vocabulary of 28,996 pieces.

The output shows something that surprises most people. The model never sees the word Tokenization. It sees three pieces, To, ##ken, and ##ization, where ## means "glued to the piece before". The second line is what the model actually receives: one integer per piece, plus 101 and 102 at the ends, which are the special [CLS] and [SEP] markers for the start and end of the text. Module 2 explains why splitting words this way is a good idea.

#Step 3: Run a named-entity model

Now the full model. This downloads about 260 MB the first time, which takes a few seconds on Colab:

Each line is one entity: its type (person, location, organization, or MISC for everything else), the model's confidence, the text, and the character positions where it starts and ends. Check one: text[61:70] is 'Safaricom'. Those positions matter, because they let you highlight or redact the exact characters in the original text.

Before the results, Colab prints a line like Device set to use cpu, or cuda:0 on a GPU runtime. That's the pipeline telling you where the model is running.

🧪 Try it yourself

Run the pipeline on three sentences of your own. Include a name that's also a place, such as "Jordan visited Jordan", and a company that's also a fruit. Write down one result that's wrong. You'll find out why in Module 4.

#Step 4: The errors you'll meet on a first run

A misspelled model name. Model ids are case-sensitive, and the error doesn't suggest a fix:

Copy the id from the model's page on the Hub (there's a copy button next to the name) instead of typing it.

KeyError: 'entity_group'. If you leave out aggregation_strategy, the pipeline returns one dict per piece instead of per entity, and those dicts call the label entity, with values like B-PER and I-PER. Code written for grouped output then crashes on the missing key. Either add aggregation_strategy="first" or read entity["entity"].

A download that can't connect. Errors mentioning ConnectionError or Max retries exceeded mean the runtime couldn't reach the Hub. Rerun the cell; if it keeps failing, check status.huggingface.co (opens in a new tab).

📝 Note

If you print a whole result with print(ner(text)), the scores may appear as np.float32(0.9990412). That's NumPy 2 showing you the number's type. Format it with :.3f as above, or convert it with float().

#Step 5: Downloads are cached

Run the pipeline cell a second time. It starts almost instantly, because the files are now stored in a cache on the runtime's disk. This cell lists what's there:

The cache lives on the Colab machine, not in your Drive. A new runtime starts with an empty cache, so the first run of each day downloads again. That's normal.

#Step 6: One cell that proves it all works

Add this as the last cell of your setup notebook. It runs a sentence with a known answer and stops with an AssertionError if the model gives anything else:

On a GPU runtime the last word is cuda:0. When you see both lines, your setup is done: scikit-learn, the tokenizer, the model, and the cache all work.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1The tokenizer turns "Tokenization is unbelievably useful." into 13 ids, but the sentence has 4 words and a period. Where do the extra ids come from?

  • Then there would be dozens of ids, not 13.

  • Tokenization becomes 3 pieces and unbelievably becomes 5, and ids 101 and 102 mark the start and end.

  • This tokenizer drops spaces; the ## prefix is how it records that a piece continues a word.

Show answer

B. Tokenization becomes 3 pieces and unbelievably becomes 5, and ids 101 and 102 mark the start and end.

2Your loop prints entity['entity_group'] and crashes with KeyError: 'entity_group'. What's the most likely cause?

  • Then the list would be empty and the loop body would never run, so there'd be no error.

  • Ungrouped output is one dict per piece, with labels like B-PER under the key entity.

  • pipeline() doesn't return until the download is finished.

Show answer

B. Ungrouped output is one dict per piece, with labels like B-PER under the key entity.

3You open your notebook the next morning and the pipeline cell spends a while downloading again. Why?

  • The Hub doesn't control your disk. The cache is just files.

  • The cache lives on the Colab machine, which is replaced when you reconnect after a break.

Show answer

B. The cache lives on the Colab machine, which is replaced when you reconnect after a break.

Key takeaways

  • A setup is proven when real text produces sensible output, not when imports succeed.
  • AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained and pipeline(..., model=...) take a Hub id such as dslim/distilbert-NER; copy ids rather than typing them.
  • Tokenizers split rare words into pieces and add special tokens, so the model sees integers, not words.
  • With aggregation_strategy, the NER pipeline returns one dict per entity, with entity_group, score, word, start, and end.
  • Downloads are cached on the runtime's disk and disappear with the runtime.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Predict what survives a session restart, a deleted runtime, and an idle timeout.
  • Set up each course notebook with the same first cell, and save files to Drive when they must outlive the runtime.
  • Use seeds so a split or a training run gives the same result twice.
  • Read a Python traceback from the last line up, and work through a short checklist when you're stuck.
  • Choose text that is safe to process and share, and keep tokens and personal data out of notebooks.

A notebook that worked perfectly on Friday fails on Monday at the third cell:

Nothing in cell 3 changed. On Friday, vocabulary existed because you'd built it in a cell you later deleted, and the variable stayed in memory until the runtime ended. Monday's fresh runtime has no memory of it. Notebooks let you run cells in any order, which is great for experimenting and terrible for knowing whether your notebook really works. This lesson is about habits that close that gap.

#What each kind of reset keeps

Colab has three ways to lose state, and they don't lose the same things:

What happens Variables in memory Files in /content, installs, model cache The notebook itself
Runtime › Restart session Lost Kept Kept
Runtime › Disconnect and delete runtime Lost Lost Kept
Idle timeout, or the free tier's maximum session length (at most 12 hours) Lost Lost Kept

The notebook file lives in your Drive, so it always survives. Everything else lives on a temporary virtual machine.

The habit that catches hidden state: before you call a notebook finished, choose Runtime › Restart session and run all. If anything depends on a deleted cell or on running cells out of order, it fails now, while you still remember why.

#One notebook per lesson, with the same first cell

Make a Drive folder called NLP course and keep one notebook per lesson in it, named so they sort in order: nlp-m2-l2-tokenizer.ipynb, nlp-m3-l2-ticket-triage.ipynb. Start every notebook with a cell like this:

Printing versions at the top costs nothing and explains a lot later. If a classmate gets a different number from the same notebook, the version lines are the first thing to compare. Use Insert › Text cell to add headings between steps; a notebook with headings is much easier to come back to.

#Save files that must outlive the runtime

Anything your code writes to /content disappears with the runtime. To keep a file, mount your Drive and save it there:

The first time, Colab asks you to allow access to your Drive. After that, /content/drive/MyDrive is your Drive, and files saved there stay. The notebook itself saves automatically; File › Download › Download .ipynb gives you a copy on your own computer.

#Seeds make results repeatable

Many steps in NLP involve randomness: shuffling data, splitting it into training and test sets, initializing model weights. Without a seed you get different numbers every run, and you can't tell whether a change you made helped or whether the dice just rolled differently.

The three unseeded splits usually differ from each other; the seeded ones are identical every time, on every computer with the same library versions. In scikit-learn, pass random_state= to anything that shuffles. For PyTorch and transformers, from transformers import set_seed and set_seed(0) seeds Python, NumPy, and PyTorch in one call. Even with seeds, GPU results can differ from CPU results in the last decimal places, so compare to two or three decimals, not ten.

#Read a traceback from the bottom up

Errors from transformers can be forty lines long, most of it inside library code you didn't write. The useful part is almost always at the bottom: the last line names the error type and says what went wrong, and the lowest line that mentions your cell tells you where. Here's a classic from Module 3:

The last line says it plainly: transform wanted an iterable of documents and got one string. A string is itself iterable (character by character), which is why scikit-learn checks for this. The fix is vectorizer.transform(["refund my card"]), a list holding one document.

When the last line doesn't make the fix obvious, work through this:

When you ask for help (a classmate, the Hugging Face forums (opens in a new tab), a search engine), include the last line of the error, the smallest piece of code that causes it, and your version cell's output. Most questions answer themselves while you're cutting the code down.

#Privacy: what text belongs in a notebook

Every example in this course is made up: invented support tickets, invented names, sentences written for the lesson. Keep your own experiments the same way.

  • Don't process real people's private text. Classmates' messages, school records, someone's emails, or anything with phone numbers and addresses stays out, even if a model would handle it well.
  • Remember that outputs travel with the notebook. If you share a notebook, everyone sees every printed result. Edit › Clear all outputs before sharing removes them.
  • Know where text goes. A model you download with from_pretrained runs on your Colab runtime; your sentences aren't sent to Hugging Face. Hosted APIs are different: text you send to them leaves your machine, which matters in later modules.
  • Tokens and keys go in Secrets, never in cells, as in the setup lesson.

⚠️ Watch out

Models make confident mistakes. The entity model from the last lesson labels the first "Washington" in "Washington signed the treaty in Washington." as a location, with a score of 0.968. A score is not a guarantee, so never let a model's output decide something about a real person without a human checking it. Module 7 is about measuring exactly this kind of failure.

#Make Colab comfortable to use

  • Zoom with Ctrl and + (Cmd and + on a Mac) to enlarge code and output together.
  • Tools › Settings has a theme choice (light, dark, or adaptive) and editor options such as line numbers.
  • Tools › Command palette lets you type the name of any menu command instead of finding it with a mouse.
  • Tools › Keyboard shortcuts lists, and lets you change, every shortcut.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You install a package with %pip, download a model, and create a variable texts. Then you choose Runtime › Restart session. What's left?

  • That's Disconnect and delete runtime. A restart only ends the Python process.

  • Files on disk survive a restart; variables in memory don't.

  • A restart starts a fresh Python process, so every variable is gone.

Show answer

B. Files on disk survive a restart; variables in memory don't.

2vectorizer.transform("refund my card") raises ValueError: Iterable over raw text documents expected, string object received. What's the fix?

  • The vectorizer is fine. Refitting would also change its vocabulary.

  • transform expects a collection of documents, even when there's only one.

  • The text is already lowercase, and case has nothing to do with this error.

Show answer

B. transform expects a collection of documents, even when there's only one.

3Your test accuracy is 0.82 on one run and 0.76 on the next, with no code changes. What should you check first?

  • Hardware faults don't usually show up as a small, plausible change in accuracy.

  • Without seeds, a different split each run gives different scores.

  • Where the file is saved doesn't affect the numbers it computes.

Show answer

B. Without seeds, a different split each run gives different scores.

Key takeaways

  • A session restart loses variables; deleting the runtime (or timing out) also loses files, installs, and the model cache. The notebook in Drive always survives.
  • Before calling a notebook finished, choose Runtime › Restart session and run all.
  • Start every notebook with the same setup cell: imports, a seed, and printed versions.
  • Save files you need later to /content/drive/MyDrive, not /content.
  • Read tracebacks from the bottom. Ask for help with the error's last line, a minimal example, and your versions.
  • Work with made-up or public text, clear outputs before sharing, and keep tokens in Secrets.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Use Unicode normalization and case folding to make visually identical strings compare equal, and say what that costs.
  • Compare whitespace, regex, and subword tokenization on the same messy sentence.
  • Explain how a subword vocabulary can spell words it has never seen.
  • Build one-hot, count, and TF-IDF representations with scikit-learn and say what each one can't capture.
  • Explain why a word's meaning can come from the words around it, and why one vector per word isn't enough for words like bank.

A café's support search has two bugs. Someone searches for cafe and gets nothing, because the tickets say "Café", "CAFÉ!", and "café". Someone else searches for bank and gets complaints about the riverside terrace mixed in with complaints about bank transfers. The first bug is the computer seeing differences that don't matter. The second is the computer missing a difference that does. Every choice in this lesson moves you between those two failures.

#Normalization decides which strings count as the same

To a computer, text is a sequence of Unicode code points, and the same visible word can be spelled with different code points. The accent in café can be one character (é) or two (e followed by a combining accent mark). They look identical and compare unequal.

NFC normalization rewrites both into the same canonical form, so they compare equal. From there you choose how far to go:

lower() handles everyday capitals. casefold() goes further and turns German ß into ss. NFKD also folds "compatibility" characters, so full-width letters and the ﬁ ligature become plain ASCII, and splits accented letters so strip_accents can drop the marks.

Each step merges strings that used to be different, and some of those differences carried meaning. Lowercasing makes "US" and "us" the same token, and "Apple" the company the same as the fruit. The rule this course follows: normalize aggressively for counting and search, but keep the original text for anything where case and accents are evidence, like entity recognition in Module 4.

#Tokenization: deciding where one token ends

Splitting on spaces is the obvious first try, and punctuation stays glued to words:

The whitespace split makes twice?! and it. into tokens that will never match twice or it. The regex \w+|[^\w\s] means "a run of word characters, or a single character that's neither a word character nor a space". It separates punctuation, and it also breaks don't into don, ', t, C++ into three tokens, and $4.50 into four. No regex handles every case; you choose rules that suit your text. Code snippets, prices, and emails each need their own.

#Subwords: a fixed vocabulary that can spell anything

Whatever your rules, a word-level vocabulary has a hard problem. New words keep arriving: names, typos, slang, product codes. A word the vocabulary has never seen has to become a single [UNK] (unknown) token, and everything about it is lost. Characters fix that (any word can be spelled) but make sequences several times longer, and single letters carry little meaning.

Subword tokenizers sit in between. Common words get a single token; rare words are spelled from a few reusable pieces. Two families dominate:

  • Byte-pair encoding (BPE), used by GPT models, starts with single characters (or bytes) and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, until the vocabulary reaches its target size. You'll build one in the next lesson.
  • WordPiece, used by BERT, learns its vocabulary in a similar way. When it tokenizes, it splits each word greedily: take the longest piece from the start of the word that's in the vocabulary, then repeat on what's left. Pieces that continue a word are written with ##.

Step through WordPiece's greedy loop on a tiny vocabulary:

The inner loop shrinks end until word[start:end] is in the vocabulary, so un wins only after the seven longer candidates fail. Notice that happy is in the vocabulary but never used: in the middle of a word, only ## pieces are allowed.

Here are two real tokenizers on the same sentence. Run this in Colab:

GPT-2's BPE marks a leading space with Ġ instead of marking continuations with ##, and its larger vocabulary keeps unbelievably whole. Both can encode any string you give them, without an [UNK]. Different models split differently, which is why you always use the tokenizer that was trained with the model.

#Four ways to turn tokens into numbers

A model needs numbers. These are the classic choices, from simplest to richest:

  1. One-hot: each vocabulary word gets its own position, and a word is a vector of zeros with a single 1 at that position. Every pair of different words is equally different, so cat is as far from kitten as from invoice.
  2. Counts (bag of words): add up the one-hot vectors of a document's words. Simple and often surprisingly good, but word order is gone.
  3. TF-IDF: counts reweighted so that words appearing in many documents count less.
  4. Embeddings: short, dense vectors (hundreds of numbers instead of tens of thousands) learned from data, where words used in similar ways end up close together.

Here's what counts and TF-IDF give for four support messages:

Read the idf column. scikit-learn computes idf as ln((1 + n) / (1 + df)) + 1, where n is the number of documents and df is how many contain the word. the is in all four messages, so its idf is the minimum, 1.0. card is in two, so 1.51. Words found in only one message get 1.92. Each count is multiplied by its idf and then the whole row is scaled to length 1, which is why the last column is smaller.

Even so, the still has the biggest weight here, because it appears twice. IDF reduces common words; it doesn't remove them. Passing stop_words="english" or sublinear_tf=True (which uses 1 + log(count)) are the usual fixes. The last line shows the limit every bag of words shares: dog bites man and man bites dog get identical vectors.

#Meaning from the company a word keeps

None of the first three representations knows that refund and money back mean nearly the same thing. Embeddings get there through an old idea, the distributional hypothesis: words that appear in similar contexts have similar meanings. If latte and espresso both keep showing up next to ordered, cup, and hot, a method that turns each word's neighbours into a vector will put them close together. In the next lesson you'll build exactly that from a co-occurrence table.

That approach gives each word one vector, and that's the second bug from the start of the lesson. bank gets one vector that's a blend of its river and money senses. Transformers fix this with contextual embeddings: the vector for bank is computed from the whole sentence, so it comes out different in "the bank of the river" and "the bank approved my loan". Module 4 shows those vectors pulling apart.

#Common mistakes

⚠️ Watch out

Fitting a vectorizer on the query. fit_transform learns a new vocabulary from whatever you give it. Call it on a search query and you get a vector in a different space from your documents:

The query was given a two-word vocabulary of its own, so its vectors have 2 columns instead of 15. Fit once on the documents, then call vectorizer.transform([query]). (Worse, that second fit_transform also replaced the vectorizer's vocabulary, so doc_vectors no longer matches it either.)

⚠️ Watch out

Lowercasing text before a cased model. The entity model in this course is cased: Apple and apple, Jordan and jordan look different to it, and that difference is evidence. Lowercasing for search is fine; lowercasing before running the model throws that evidence away.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Two tickets say "CAFÉ" and "cafe". Which steps make them the same token?

  • That gives "café" and "cafe", which still differ by the accent.

  • NFKD separates the accent from the letter, the filter drops it, and case folding handles the capitals.

  • Splitting decides where tokens end; it doesn't change the characters.

Show answer

B. NFKD separates the accent from the letter, the filter drops it, and case folding handles the capitals.

2In the TF-IDF table, the has the lowest idf yet the highest tf-idf in the second message. Why?

  • Ranking isn't involved; the weights come from counts and idf.

  • IDF shrinks common words but doesn't cancel a higher count. Stop words or sublinear tf deal with this.

  • The +1 terms are deliberate, so a word found in every document still gets idf 1, not 0.

Show answer

B. IDF shrinks common words but doesn't cancel a higher count. Stop words or sublinear tf deal with this.

3A WordPiece vocabulary contains un, ##do, and ##able but not undoable. What does greedy longest-match produce for undoable?

  • The longest known piece at the start is un, then ##do, then ##able.

  • WordPiece gives up only when some part of the word can't be matched at all.

  • That piece isn't in the vocabulary, so it can't be chosen.

Show answer

A. The longest known piece at the start is un, then ##do, then ##able.

4Why does a static word embedding struggle with bank?

  • Length doesn't matter; every vocabulary word gets a vector.

  • Static embeddings are a lookup table, so context can't change the vector. Contextual embeddings fix this.

  • TF-IDF and embeddings are separate representations.

Show answer

B. Static embeddings are a lookup table, so context can't change the vector. Contextual embeddings fix this.

Key takeaways

  • Normalization (NFC or NFKD, case folding, accent stripping) merges strings that look the same, and every merge can also erase a difference that mattered.
  • Tokenization rules are choices. Whitespace keeps punctuation attached; regexes break prices, contractions, and code.
  • Subword tokenizers (BPE, WordPiece) keep common words whole and spell rare words from pieces, so they never need [UNK] for ordinary text. Always use the tokenizer that came with the model.
  • One-hot and counts treat all words as equally different. TF-IDF downweights common words. Embeddings put similar words close together.
  • Fit a vectorizer once on your documents, then transform new text.
  • One vector per word blends a word's meanings; contextual embeddings give one vector per occurrence.

  • Speech and Language Processing, Jurafsky and Martin (opens in a new tab): the free textbook draft. Chapter 2, "Words and Tokens", covers normalization and BPE; Chapter 5, "Embeddings", covers TF-IDF and learned word vectors.

What you'll learn

  • Train a BPE tokenizer by repeatedly merging the most frequent pair of adjacent symbols.
  • Use the learned merges to split words the tokenizer has never seen.
  • Build a vocabulary with special tokens, encode a batch of sentences into padded ids with an attention mask, and decode them back.
  • Count which words appear near which, weight the counts with PPMI, and compress them into dense vectors with SVD.
  • Plot the vectors and use cosine similarity to find each word's nearest neighbours.

You'll build the two halves of the pipeline from the last lesson, starting from nothing but 18 sentences: a subword tokenizer like the ones GPT models use, and a set of word vectors learned only from which words appear together. Here's where it ends up. The tokenizer, after 40 merges, splits a word it never saw in training:

And the word vectors, squeezed into two dimensions, put money words in one group, river words in another, and bank between them, because it was used both ways.

Make a new Colab notebook called nlp-m2-l2-tokenizer.ipynb and add each step as a new cell. Everything here uses only Python, NumPy, and matplotlib.

#Step 1: A tiny corpus and a cleaning function

Half of these sentences use bank for money, half for a river's edge. That's on purpose: it's the ambiguity from the start of the module.

tokenize does the normalization from the last lesson (strip accents, case-fold) and keeps runs of letters and digits, which drops punctuation. Real BPE tokenizers keep punctuation and spaces; dropping them keeps this build small.

#Step 2: Train BPE by merging the most frequent pair

BPE starts with every word spelled as single characters, plus an end-of-word marker </w> so the tokenizer can tell a piece at the end of a word from the same letters in the middle. Then it repeats one move: count every pair of neighbouring symbols across the corpus, weighted by how often each word appears, and merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol.

Read the merges in order. The first is h + e, because the appears 29 times and he, her, checking add more. Next he + </w> forms a word ending, then t + he</w> builds the whole word the. Frequent words become single tokens quickly; bank gets there by merge 11 (scroll the full list by changing step < 10 to step < 40). Rare words stay in pieces, but the pieces they share, like ed</w> and ing, get merged because they add up across many words.

📝 Note

pairs.most_common(1) breaks ties by whichever pair was counted first. Real tokenizers use a fixed rule for ties too; without one, two training runs on the same text could give different vocabularies.

#Step 3: Split words the tokenizer has never seen

To tokenize a new word, start from characters again and replay the merges in the order they were learned:

None of these words is in the corpus. loaned comes out as loan + ed</w>, two pieces that carry meaning. riverbank shows why the end-of-word marker matters: the tokenizer learned river</w>, a complete word, so river in the middle of a compound only gets as far as riv + er. And zebra falls back to single letters, which is how BPE guarantees it can spell anything, as long as every character was seen in training.

#Step 4: A vocabulary of ids, with padding

A model needs integers. The vocabulary is two special tokens, then every starting character, then one new token per merge:

Two things to notice. The letter z never appeared in training, so it isn't in the alphabet and becomes [UNK] (id 1), and the decoded sentence silently loses it. GPT-2 avoids this by starting from the 256 possible bytes instead of characters, so every string is covered. Second, the shorter sentence is padded with [PAD] (id 0) to the length of the longer one, so the batch is a rectangle, and attention_mask marks which positions are real. Hugging Face tokenizers return the same two lists, under the same names.

#Step 5: Count which words appear near which

Now the second half: vectors that capture meaning. The plan is the distributional hypothesis made literal. For each word, count how often every other word appears within two positions of it. Function words like the appear next to everything and say nothing about meaning, so they're dropped first.

Each row of cooc is a word's context profile. bank's row mixes river (5 times), water, and grassy with loan and friday. That row already is a vector for bank, 50 numbers long, but it's noisy and mostly zeros.

#Step 6: Reweight with PPMI and compress with SVD

Raw counts favour frequent words. Pointwise mutual information asks a better question: does river appear near bank more often than you'd expect if words were scattered at random? PMI = log(P(word, context) / (P(word) × P(context))). Negative values are unreliable with this little data, so PPMI (positive PMI) clips them to zero.

Then singular value decomposition rewrites the matrix as a sum of patterns ordered from strongest to weakest. Keeping only the first few gives each word a short dense vector that captures its main patterns of use. This is the idea behind latent semantic analysis, and GloVe vectors are a close relative.

Now plot two groups of words, plus bank:

Nothing told the program which sentences were about money. The two groups come purely from which words shared neighbours. bank sits between them, because its context row is a mix of both. It's closer to the river side, since more of its 12 uses in this corpus are river uses. That's the limit of one vector per word, drawn as a picture.

#Step 7: Nearest neighbours by cosine similarity

Two dimensions are for plotting. For finding similar words, keep more: here, ten. Cosine similarity compares directions, ignoring length: divide each vector by its length, then take dot products.

savings lands next to account and loan. bank's neighbours come from both senses at once. With 18 sentences the lists are noisy; the same recipe on millions of sentences gives the familiar results where coffee sits near tea. Module 3 uses cosine similarity again, on whole documents.

#The finished program

Here are both halves in one file, the version to keep. It needs corpus from Step 1 and STOP from Step 5; paste those two lists above it if you run it on its own.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the tokenizer add </w> to the end of every word before training?

  • Words still have different lengths; one marker is added to each.

  • That's why riverbank can't use the learned river</w> token in the middle of the word.

  • The words were already separated by tokenize; the marker is for BPE.

Show answer

B. That's why riverbank can't use the learned river</w> token in the middle of the word.

2The batch's second sentence decodes as "a ebra swam in the river". Why is the z gone?

  • decode only skips ids 0 and 1, which are [PAD] and [UNK].

  • A byte-level base alphabet, as in GPT-2, would have covered it.

  • Padding is added at the end of the shorter sequence, never inside it.

Show answer

B. A byte-level base alphabet, as in GPT-2, would have covered it.

3Why use PPMI instead of raw co-occurrence counts before SVD?

  • The matrix keeps the same shape; only the values change.

  • A word that appears everywhere gets large raw counts with everything, but a low PMI.

  • SVD works on any real matrix.

Show answer

B. A word that appears everywhere gets large raw counts with everything, but a low PMI.

Key takeaways

  • BPE training is one loop: count adjacent pairs (weighted by word frequency), merge the most frequent, repeat. The merge list is the tokenizer.
  • Encoding replays the merges in order, so unseen words split into known pieces; characters never seen in training become [UNK] unless the base alphabet is bytes.
  • Batches are padded to a rectangle, and an attention mask marks the real positions.
  • Co-occurrence counts, reweighted with PPMI and compressed with SVD, give dense word vectors in which words used alike end up close.
  • One vector per word blends senses: bank lands between money and river.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Train with 10, 40, and 100 merges and print how many tokens encode produces for the whole corpus each time. More merges means fewer, longer tokens.
  • Start from bytes, as GPT-2 does: spell each word as its UTF-8 bytes with list(word.encode("utf-8")), and give each merge a new integer id instead of joining strings. Then any text works, zebra and emoji included. This is the version Karpathy builds in the video.
  • Change window to 1 and to 5, and watch how the neighbour lists change. Small windows tend to group words that play the same grammatical role; large windows group words by topic.
  • Add six sentences about cafés and drinks, and check that a third group appears with more dimensions.

#Further reading

  • Karpathy's minbpe (opens in a new tab): a clean, short implementation of byte-level BPE with the GPT-4 split pattern, written to be read.
  • Hugging Face LLM Course: Byte-Pair Encoding tokenization (opens in a new tab): the same algorithm with a worked example, then how the tokenizers library does it at scale.
  • Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 5: Embeddings (opens in a new tab): PPMI, cosine similarity, and how learned embeddings like word2vec relate to count-based ones.

What you'll learn

  • Measure how vocabulary size trades off against unknown words on text the vocabulary never saw.
  • Use n-grams to recover some of the word order a bag of words throws away.
  • Write a single regex that tokenizes prices, emails, contractions, and language names correctly.
  • Reproduce scikit-learn's TF-IDF numbers exactly with NumPy.
  • Pad and truncate a batch of ids the way Hugging Face tokenizers do.
  • Show with a chart why a BPE vocabulary compresses its training text better than new text.

Each exercise is a small, complete program. Try it in a fresh Colab cell before opening the solution; the sample output tells you when you've got it.

#Warm-up: which strings are equal?

Before running this, predict for each pair whether it's equal after NFC normalization, and whether it's equal after NFKC plus casefold().

Only the last pair survives NFC alone, because NFC fixes how a character is encoded but never changes case or unpacks the ﬁ ligature. NFKC unpacks the ligature, and casefold() handles both the capitals and ß.

#Exercise 1: Vocabulary size against unknown words

Build a vocabulary from six training tickets, keeping only words that appear at least min_count times, plus an [UNK] token. Then measure the out-of-vocabulary (OOV) rate: the share of words in two held-out tickets that aren't in the vocabulary. Compare min_count=1 with min_count=2.

Need a hint?

Counter(word for text in texts for word in text.split()) counts every word. Keep the ones with a count of at least min_count, and put [UNK] at id 0.

Show solution

Dropping rare words cut the vocabulary by more than half and pushed the OOV rate from 17% to 42%. Notice crashed is unknown even though crashes was seen: a word-level vocabulary can't share anything between the two, which is exactly what subword tokenizers fix.

#Exercise 2: Put some word order back with bigrams

"not good, very bad" and "not bad, very good" mean opposite things. Show that CountVectorizer() gives them identical vectors, then that CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2)) doesn't, and print the features that differ.

Need a hint?

Fit on both reviews, call .toarray(), and unpack the two rows as a, b. Zip get_feature_names_out() with a and b to find positions where they differ.

Show solution

Bigrams like not good capture local order. Notice bad very and good very: the comma is dropped before n-grams are formed, so bigrams cross punctuation. The cost is size. Real vocabularies grow several-fold with bigrams, which is why min_df usually comes along with them.

#Exercise 3: A tokenizer for prices, emails, and C++

Write smart_tokenize(text) using one compiled regex so that this sentence:

becomes:

Need a hint?

re.findall tries the alternatives of A|B|C in order at each position, so put the most specific patterns (email, money, C++) before the general word pattern, and a catch-all [^\w\s] last. With re.VERBOSE you can add comments, but a literal # must be written \#. Make sure the email pattern doesn't swallow the sentence's final period.

Show solution

The email pattern ends with (?:\.\w+)+, one or more groups of a dot followed by letters, so the period after .org can't match: no letter follows it. Order is doing most of the work. Move the word pattern to the top and C++ turns back into C, +, +.

#Exercise 4: TF-IDF with NumPy, matched to scikit-learn

Using CountVectorizer for the counts and NumPy for everything else, compute TF-IDF for these three documents and check with np.allclose that you match TfidfVectorizer() exactly.

Need a hint?

Three steps: document frequency is (counts > 0).sum(axis=0); idf is log((1 + n) / (1 + df)) + 1; multiply counts by idf, then divide each row by its length (np.linalg.norm(..., axis=1, keepdims=True)).

Show solution

my and order appear in every document, so their idf is exactly 1. Every other word appears once and gets ln(4/2) + 1 ≈ 1.693. If you forget the row normalization, allclose prints False; that step is easy to miss.

#Exercise 5: Pad and truncate a batch

Write pad_batch(batch, max_length, pad_id=0) that returns {"input_ids": ..., "attention_mask": ...}. Pad every sequence to the length of the longest one, but never beyond max_length. When a sequence is too long, cut it but keep its last id, because that's the [SEP] marker (id 102) the model expects at the end.

Need a hint?

The target length is min(longest sequence, max_length). For a sequence that's too long, take ids[:length - 1] + [ids[-1]].

Show solution

This is what tokenizer(texts, padding=True, truncation=True, max_length=6) does for a BERT-style tokenizer. Truncation removes words from the end of the text, and [SEP] is still added after them. Truncation also loses information silently, which Module 5 deals with.

#Exercise 6: Chart how BPE compresses old and new text

Train BPE on ten support tickets with up to 200 merges. For 0, 10, 25, 50, 100, 150, and 200 merges, measure the average number of tokens per word on the training text and on two new tickets, and plot both as lines.

Need a hint?

Reuse merge_pieces and the training loop from the build-along, keeping the merges in a list. Then merges[:k] is the tokenizer you'd have after k merges, so you train once and slice. Stop training early if no pairs are left.

Show solution

Training stops before 200: once every training word is a single token there are no pairs left to merge, and the training line sits at exactly 1.0. New text never gets there, because words like parcel and login were never seen and still need several pieces. The gap between the lines is the tokenizer overfitting its training text, and it's one reason real tokenizers are trained on huge, varied corpora.

#Challenge: Write a WordPiece tokenizer

Write tokenize(text, vocab) that first splits text into words and punctuation, then splits each word with WordPiece's greedy longest-match rule: take the longest prefix in the vocabulary, then the longest ## continuation, and so on. If any part of a word can't be matched, the whole word becomes [UNK]. With this 18-token vocabulary, your function should reproduce what the real BERT tokenizer did with this sentence in Module 1:

The three lines are for "Tokenization is unbelievably useful.", "tokens reuse usefully", and "Tokenization is zany.".

Need a hint?

The trace in the Notes lesson is most of the answer. To split words from punctuation, use re.findall(r"\w+|[^\w\s]", text). Python's while ... else is handy here: the else block runs only if the loop ended without break, which is exactly the "no piece matched" case.

Show solution

usefully shows the greedy rule at work: useful is the longest known prefix, leaving ##ly. zany fails at the first letter, so the whole word becomes one [UNK]; BERT never emits half a word plus an unknown piece. The real tokenizer does a little more before WordPiece (it puts spaces around Chinese characters and, for uncased models, lowercases and strips accents), and it caps words at 100 characters, as max_chars does here.

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Compute cosine similarity by hand and explain why it suits text better than straight-line distance.
  • Search a set of documents by turning the query into a TF-IDF vector and ranking by cosine similarity.
  • Explain how multinomial naive Bayes and logistic regression turn word counts into a label.
  • Train both classifiers in scikit-learn pipelines and inspect what each class has learned.
  • Read a confusion matrix and per-class precision and recall, and know when accuracy misleads.

A small online shop routes its support email with one rule: if the message contains card, send it to Billing. It works for a few days. Then "The app crashes when I open the gift card screen" lands in Billing, and so does "My birthday card arrived torn". Single keywords fail in both directions: they match words that mean something else here, and they miss messages that say the same thing in different words, like money back instead of refund.

This module replaces the keyword with two tools. Similarity finds past tickets that look like a new one. Classification learns a label from many examples instead of one word.

#Cosine similarity compares direction, not size

Two texts about the same thing use the same words in roughly the same proportions. A long complaint about a double charge and a short one point the same way in word-count space; the long one is just further out. So instead of measuring the distance between the two points, measure the angle between the vectors. That's cosine similarity:

cos(a, b) = (a · b) / (‖a‖ ‖b‖)

The dot product a · b adds up the products of matching counts, so it's large when both texts use the same words. Dividing by the two lengths removes the effect of text length. For count or TF-IDF vectors, which have no negative entries, the result runs from 0 (no words in common) to 1 (identical proportions).

The doubled text has cosine 1.0 with the original: same direction, same meaning. Straight-line distance puts it 2.0 away, nearly as far as the unrelated parcel message (2.449). Distance punishes length; cosine ignores it. The 0.25 between the card text and the parcel text comes entirely from the shared word my, which is why stop words and TF-IDF weighting matter for search.

#Search is ranking documents by similarity to the query

Here are 18 past tickets with the team's labels. To search them, fit a TF-IDF vectorizer on the tickets once, turn each query into a vector with the same vectorizer, and rank tickets by cosine similarity.

The first two queries work well, and their top matches all carry the right label, which hints at the next idea: a new ticket probably deserves the label of the tickets it most resembles. The third query shows the limit of word overlap. money back means refund, but no ticket shares a single word with it, so every score is 0. Fixing that takes vectors that place refund near money back: sentence embeddings from a transformer, which Module 6 compares with TF-IDF for retrieval.

#Naive Bayes: which class makes these words most likely?

Multinomial naive Bayes imagines that each class writes tickets by drawing words from its own bag. Billing's bag is full of refund, charge, and invoice; Shipping's has parcel, late, and courier. To label a new ticket, ask which bag was most likely to produce its words:

score(class) = log P(class) + Σ log P(word | class)

The probabilities come from counting words in each class's training tickets. Logs turn a product of many small probabilities into a sum, which avoids numbers too small for the computer to store. The "naive" part is treating each word as independent of the others, which is false (double and charge go together) but works well enough to have filtered spam for decades.

refund pushes strongly toward billing (−1.61 against −3.00), but late and parcel push harder toward shipping, so shipping wins. A word that never appeared in a class's training tickets would get probability 0 and a log of minus infinity, vetoing that class outright. Naive Bayes avoids that with smoothing: MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0) adds one imaginary occurrence of every word to every class.

#Logistic regression: learn a weight for every word

Logistic regression takes the other route. It gives every word a weight for each class and adds up weight × TF-IDF value, plus a bias, to get a score per class. A softmax turns the scores into probabilities. Training adjusts the weights to make the correct labels as probable as possible, so the model learns which words matter instead of counting them.

Train both in pipelines and test them on seven tickets neither has seen:

A pipeline bundles the vectorizer and the classifier, so fit learns the vocabulary from the training tickets only and predict reuses it, which rules out the fit-on-the-query mistake from Module 2. Both models miss the same ticket, and it's a fair miss: "charged for a parcel that never arrived" is a billing complaint about a shipping problem.

Logistic regression's weights tell you what it learned, and its probabilities tell you how sure it was:

The top words look sensible, apart from was sitting near the top for billing: with 18 training tickets, the model picks up accidents of phrasing as well as real signal. And it was nearly a coin flip between billing and shipping on the misclassified ticket. A low top probability is a useful signal: in the next lesson, low-confidence tickets go to a human.

#Evaluate on tickets the model never saw

Scoring a model on its own training tickets measures memory, not skill. Hold out a test set, predict it, and compare. Accuracy is the share correct. It hides which mistakes happen, so also read the confusion matrix, with one row per true label and one column per predicted label:

The diagonal counts correct answers. The 1 in row billing, column shipping is the misread ticket. From the matrix come two numbers per class:

  • Precision: of the tickets predicted shipping, what share really were? 2 of 3, so 0.67.
  • Recall: of the real billing tickets, what share were found? 2 of 3, so 0.67.

F1 is their harmonic mean. Macro avg averages the classes equally; weighted avg weights them by how many test tickets each has. With seven test tickets, one mistake moves accuracy by 14 points, so treat these numbers as rough. The Practice lesson uses cross-validation to get steadier ones.

⚠️ Watch out

Accuracy on unbalanced classes. If 90 of 100 tickets are billing, a "model" that always says billing scores 90% accuracy and never finds a single shipping problem. Always compare against that baseline (scikit-learn's DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent") computes it), and read recall for the small classes.

⚠️ Watch out

Letting the test set leak into training. Calling TfidfVectorizer().fit_transform(all_texts) before splitting lets the test tickets shape the vocabulary and the idf weights. Worse is a duplicated ticket that lands on both sides of the split, which the model "predicts" by memory. Split first, keep the vectorizer inside a pipeline, and remove exact duplicates before splitting.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Ticket A is "refund my order" and ticket B is the same three words repeated five times. What is their cosine similarity on count vectors?

  • Cosine divides by both lengths, so length cancels out.

  • B's vector is A's times five: same direction, so the angle is zero.

  • These are plain count vectors, and even with idf, scaling every count by 5 keeps the direction.

Show answer

B. B's vector is A's times five: same direction, so the angle is zero.

2In naive Bayes, the word invoice never appeared in any shipping ticket. Without smoothing, what happens when a new ticket contains invoice?

  • An unseen word lowers a class's score; it never raises it.

  • One unseen word vetoes the class. alpha=1.0 adds pseudo-counts to prevent this.

  • scikit-learn ignores words missing from the whole vocabulary, but invoice is in it (from billing tickets).

Show answer

B. One unseen word vetoes the class. alpha=1.0 adds pseudo-counts to prevent this.

3A classifier gets 95% accuracy on a test set where 95% of tickets are billing. What should you check before celebrating?

  • Training accuracy says nothing about how the minority classes are handled.

  • Always predicting billing scores 95% too. Per-class recall shows whether the model finds anything else.

  • That's a modelling choice, not a check on whether the accuracy is meaningful.

Show answer

B. Always predicting billing scores 95% too. Per-class recall shows whether the model finds anything else.

4Why fit the vectorizer inside a pipeline instead of on all the tickets first?

  • Otherwise the test set influences the features, and the score is optimistic.

  • Speed isn't the reason; the order of fitting is.

  • It accepts sparse input either way.

Show answer

A. Otherwise the test set influences the features, and the score is optimistic.

Key takeaways

  • Cosine similarity compares the direction of two vectors, so it ignores text length. For count and TF-IDF vectors it runs from 0 to 1.
  • Search = fit a vectorizer on the documents, transform the query, rank by cosine. Word-overlap search can't match synonyms.
  • Naive Bayes adds log probabilities of each word under each class; smoothing stops unseen words from vetoing a class.
  • Logistic regression learns a weight per word per class; its coefficients show what it learned, and predict_proba shows how sure it is.
  • Evaluate on held-out text. Read the confusion matrix and per-class precision and recall, and compare accuracy against the most-frequent-class baseline.

  • scikit-learn: Classification of text documents using sparse features (opens in a new tab): an official worked example that trains and compares several text classifiers on TF-IDF features, with confusion matrices and timing.

  • Speech and Language Processing (opens in a new tab): Chapter 4 covers logistic regression for text classification and its evaluation; Appendix B covers naive Bayes.

  • Route tickets automatically only when the model is confident, and measure what that costs in coverage.

The finished tool takes a new ticket and returns a decision like this:

It labels the ticket, shows how sure it is, and pulls up similar solved cases for whoever handles it. When it isn't sure, it says so and hands the ticket to a person. You'll build it in eight steps, and the first version won't be good. Finding out why is most of the lesson.

Make a notebook called nlp-m3-l2-triage.ipynb.

#Step 1: The labelled tickets

Sixty tickets an online clothing shop might get, 15 for each of four teams. They're written to be realistic, which means messy: account appears in billing tickets ("my bank account"), shipping appears in billing ones ("billed for shipping"), and checkout belongs to both billing and technical.

#Step 2: Hold out a test set first

Before anything else touches the data, set aside a quarter of it. stratify=labels keeps the four classes in the same proportions on both sides, so the test set gets 3 or 4 tickets from each team instead of, by bad luck, none from one.

From here until Step 6, the test set stays untouched. Every decision about the model is made with training data only.

#Step 3: A first model, and its mistakes

The default choices from the Notes lesson: TF-IDF features into logistic regression, wrapped in a pipeline.

Look at what the model learned. Next to sensible words like refund and delivery sit my, how, was, for, is, the, and on. With only 45 training tickets, the accident that more account tickets happen to say my and how looks like a real pattern. Those words carry no information about the team, and they're crowding out the words that do.

#Step 4: Fix it, and prove the fix with cross-validation

Two changes. stop_words="english" removes common function words before counting. C=10 weakens logistic regression's regularization (its default penalty for large weights), letting the remaining words get larger weights; with so few examples per word, the default pulls them too close to zero.

Is the new version better? Don't ask the test set; once you choose models by their test score, it stops being an honest estimate. Ask cross-validation instead: split the training set into 5 folds, train on 4, score on the 5th, and rotate.

The mean rises by about 20 points. The individual folds bounce around a lot, because each one has only 9 tickets, so a single fold could be fooled; the mean over five is steadier, and the improved model wins or ties on every fold. Because cross_val_score refits the whole pipeline each time, the vectorizer never sees the held-out fold either.

#Step 5: Look at the confusion matrix

Now, once, score the chosen model on the test set:

Read the shipping column: shipping's recall is perfect (all 3 shipping tickets were found), but 4 tickets from other teams were also sent there, so its precision is only 3 out of 7, or 0.43. Shipping has become the model's default guess when it's unsure. Let's see which tickets those are:

Each mistake has a reason you can name. refunds is a different token from refund, which the model learned, so the PayPal ticket has almost no billing evidence (the subword idea from Module 2 would help). bank account contains account, the strongest account word. And "unsubscribe me from your marketing emails" uses words that appear in no training ticket at all. The fix for all three is more and more varied training data; no setting will invent the missing evidence.

#Step 6: Similar-case search

An agent handling a ticket wants to see how similar tickets were solved. The pipeline's vectorizer already turns text into TF-IDF vectors, so reuse it and index the training tickets with NearestNeighbors:

With metric="cosine", kneighbors returns cosine distance, which is 1 minus cosine similarity, so the code converts it back. The vectorizer drops stop words, so only refund (and weeks, which no ticket contains) can match. That's why the third result scores 0.00: no other ticket shares a word, and it's an arbitrary pick. A real tool would hide matches below a minimum similarity.

#Step 7: Only act when the model is confident

The model's top probability says how sure it is. Route a ticket automatically only when that probability clears a threshold, and send the rest to a person:

At 0.5, the model handles fewer than half the tickets, but gets every one of those right. That's the trade-off you get to choose: coverage (how much work the model takes off people) against accuracy on what it handles. With 15 test tickets, these numbers are rough; with a real inbox you'd pick the threshold from a few hundred labelled tickets.

#Step 8: The finished triage function

The second ticket only just clears the bar at 0.55, and its closest past case is an account ticket. It really is both: a technical fault in an account feature. Raise threshold to 0.6 and it goes to a person, with the password-reset ticket at the top of the similar cases, which is the most useful thing the tool can do for it.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why was the test set split off in Step 2, before choosing between the baseline and improved models?

  • The order is about what information each decision uses, not a library rule.

  • If you pick the model that scores best on the test set, that score is no longer unbiased.

  • It would run fine. It would just let test tickets influence your choice.

Show answer

B. If you pick the model that scores best on the test set, that score is no longer unbiased.

2The shipping column of the confusion matrix has 3 correct and 4 wrong predictions. What does that mean?

  • Recall is about the shipping row: all 3 real shipping tickets were found, so recall is 1.0.

  • Precision reads down the predicted column.

  • It's the reverse: shipping is its fallback guess.

Show answer

B. Precision reads down the predicted column.

3You raise the confidence threshold from 0.4 to 0.5. What happens?

  • A higher bar trades coverage for accuracy on the tickets the model keeps.

  • The threshold is applied after prediction; the model doesn't change.

  • Overall accuracy is the same; the threshold only changes which tickets go to people.

Show answer

A. A higher bar trades coverage for accuracy on the tickets the model keeps.

Key takeaways

  • Split off the test set first and stratify it. Make every modelling decision with cross-validation on the training set, then score on the test set once.
  • A model's top-weighted words are a fast diagnostic. Function words near the top mean the model is learning accidents; stop words and more data help.
  • The confusion matrix shows which mistakes happen: recall reads along a row, precision down a column.
  • The pipeline's fitted vectorizer can power nearest-neighbour search too; with metric="cosine", similarity = 1 − distance.
  • Acting only on confident predictions trades coverage for accuracy, and you choose the threshold.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a fifth team, returns, with 15 tickets of its own, and see which existing team it gets confused with.
  • Try TfidfVectorizer(analyzer="char_wb", ngram_range=(3, 5)) so refund and refunds share pieces, and compare it with cross-validation.
  • Write 20 new tickets in your own words, label them, and use them as a second test set. Scores usually drop on text written by someone else, which tells you how much the model relies on one writer's phrasing.

#Further reading

  • scikit-learn: Cross-validation (opens in a new tab): why and how to evaluate with folds, including stratified splits and the pitfalls of using the test set for model selection.
  • scikit-learn: Classification metrics (opens in a new tab): precise definitions of precision, recall, F1, and the averaging options in classification_report.
  • scikit-learn: Nearest Neighbors (opens in a new tab): the algorithms behind NearestNeighbors and when brute-force search is the right choice.

What you'll learn

  • Use pairwise cosine similarity to find near-duplicate texts.
  • Compute precision, recall, and F1 from a confusion matrix without a library, then confirm with scikit-learn.
  • Show why accuracy misleads on unbalanced classes, and use macro F1 instead.
  • Measure how much a cross-validation score changes with the shuffle.
  • Use character n-grams to make similarity robust to typos.
  • Chart how a confidence threshold trades coverage for accuracy.

Run this setup cell first. Exercises 4, 6, and the challenge use its 32 tickets; the others bring their own data.

#Warm-up: cosine similarity in your head

Predict the cosine similarity of a = [2, 1, 0] and b = [1, 1, 1] before running this. (The dot product is 3; the lengths are √5 and √3.)

3 / √15 ≈ 0.775. Doubling a to [4, 2, 0] leaves it unchanged.

#Exercise 1: Find near-duplicate tickets

Customers often send the same complaint twice. Duplicates inflate your counts, and if one copy lands in training and the other in testing, they make a model look smarter than it is. Find every pair in this inbox with TF-IDF cosine similarity of at least 0.5.

Need a hint?

cosine_similarity(X) with a single matrix returns every pair at once, as a square matrix. Loop over itertools.combinations(range(len(inbox)), 2) so each pair appears once and nothing is compared with itself.

Show solution

The first pair scores exactly 1.00: lowercasing and dropping punctuation made them identical. The threshold is a judgement call. At 0.5 the three parcel tickets group together, which is right; lower it to 0.3 and unrelated tickets that share my start to pair up.

#Exercise 2: Precision, recall, and F1 by hand

A classifier produced this confusion matrix on 30 tickets (rows are true labels, columns are predictions, in the order billing, shipping, technical):

Compute precision, recall, and F1 for each class with NumPy, then check your numbers with classification_report.

Need a hint?

Precision divides the diagonal by the column sums; recall divides it by the row sums. F1 = 2PR / (P + R). To check with scikit-learn, rebuild y_true and y_pred lists: cell [i, j] of the matrix means that many tickets with true class i and prediction j.

Show solution

Shipping is the weak class on both measures: 3 shipping tickets were called technical (hurting recall), and 2 billing tickets were called shipping (hurting precision). Technical has the opposite profile: it finds 9 of its 10 tickets, but a quarter of what it labels technical isn't.

#Exercise 3: The 90% model that finds nothing

In a test set of 20 tickets, 18 are billing and 2 are shipping. Compare a "model" that always says billing with a real one that gets 2 billing tickets wrong (calls them shipping) and finds 1 of the 2 shipping tickets. Report accuracy and macro F1 for both.

Need a hint?

Build the lists directly: y_true = ["billing"] * 18 + ["shipping"] * 2. Use accuracy_score and f1_score(..., average="macro", zero_division=0).

Show solution

Accuracy prefers the useless model. Macro F1 averages the F1 of each class equally, so the shipping class's F1 of 0 drags the always-billing model down to 0.47. When the small class is the one you care about (fraud, an outage, a safety complaint), report per-class recall and macro F1, never accuracy alone.

#Exercise 4: How much does a cross-validation score wobble?

Using the setup tickets and the pipeline TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english") + LogisticRegression(C=10), run 4-fold stratified cross-validation five times with random_state 0 to 4. Print each run's fold scores and mean.

Need a hint?

Only the random_state of StratifiedKFold(n_splits=4, shuffle=True, random_state=seed) changes between runs; the model is the same each time.

Show solution

A single 8-ticket fold can report anything from 25% to 75% for the same model. Even the averages over four folds range from 0.44 to 0.56 depending only on the shuffle. With data this small, a difference of a few points between two models is noise; report the spread, and don't trust a single split.

#Exercise 5: Make similarity survive typos

Three customers type in a hurry. Match each query to the closest of three known tickets, first with word TF-IDF, then with TfidfVectorizer(analyzer="char_wb", ngram_range=(3, 5)), and compare the scores.

Need a hint?

Fit each vectorizer on known, then compare vec.transform(queries) with vec.transform(known). char_wb makes character n-grams only inside word boundaries, padding each word with spaces.

Show solution

With words, the login query shares nothing with any ticket (cant, login, and pasword are all new tokens), so its score is 0.00 and the "match" is arbitrary. Character n-grams like pas, wor, and ord survive the typo, and closing shares clos with closes. This is the same idea as subword tokens: pieces of words generalize where whole words can't.

#Exercise 6: Chart coverage against accuracy

Get an honest probability for every setup ticket with cross_val_predict(..., method="predict_proba") (each ticket is scored by a model that never saw it). Then, for thresholds from 0.25 to 0.70 in steps of 0.05, compute coverage (share of tickets with top probability at or above the threshold) and accuracy on those tickets. Plot both against the threshold.

Need a hint?

cross_val_predict returns one row of probabilities per ticket, with columns in sorted label order, so np.array(sorted(set(labels)))[probs.argmax(axis=1)] gives the predicted labels.

Show solution

Just above 0.25 the lines cross: by 0.3 the model handles about 60% of tickets and gets about 70% of those right, against 50% when it handles everything. The accuracy line is jagged and even dips around 0.45, because at high thresholds it's measured on a handful of tickets. With 32 examples this chart is a sketch; the method is what you'd reuse on a real inbox.

#Challenge: A nearest-neighbour classifier from scratch

Similarity can label text directly: give a new ticket the most common label among its k most similar training tickets. Write knn_predict(train_texts, train_labels, test_texts, k=3) using a TF-IDF vectorizer (with English stop words) fitted on the training texts and cosine_similarity. Evaluate it with the same 4 folds as Exercise 6 (folds.split(texts, labels) gives the index arrays), and compare with KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3, metric="cosine") and logistic regression in pipelines.

Need a hint?

For each row of the similarity matrix, row.argsort()[::-1][:k] gives the k nearest training tickets. Counter(...).most_common(1)[0][0] picks the winning label. Turn texts and labels into NumPy arrays so you can index them with the fold's index arrays.

Show solution

Your version and scikit-learn's disagree on some folds, mostly because of ties. When the three neighbours have three different labels, Counter.most_common keeps the first one it counted (the nearest), while scikit-learn picks the label that comes first alphabetically. With short tickets, many similarities are exactly 0, which creates more ties. None of the three models is clearly best on 32 tickets; Exercise 4 showed that differences this small are within the noise.
