m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Describe named-entity recognition as labelling every token, and write BIO tags for a sentence.
  • Turn a sequence of BIO tags back into entities, and explain what the B tag is for.
  • Extract dates, money, and emails with rules where a pretrained model has no label for them.
  • Read the output of a token-classification pipeline, and choose an aggregation strategy that keeps words whole.
  • Follow a sentence through a transformer: tokens, ids, contextual vectors, logits, probabilities, labels.

Here's what the entity model from Module 1 does with two sentences:

In the first sentence, the same word gets two different labels, and both are right. The model didn't look Jordan up in a list. It read the words around it: Peele after it, from before it. In the second sentence it gets the first Washington wrong (a person signed the treaty), and it's confident about it. This lesson is about both halves of that: how context reaches each word, and how to find out why a model decided what it did.

#Named-entity recognition gives every token a label

Named-entity recognition (NER) finds spans of text that name things and says what kind of thing each one is. The model in this course was trained on CoNLL-2003, a collection of news articles labelled with four types: PER (people), ORG (organizations), LOC (locations), and MISC (other names, such as events, nationalities, and products).

The trick that makes NER a classification problem is to label every token, not every span. The standard scheme is BIO: B- marks the first token of an entity, I- marks a token inside one, and O marks a token outside any entity.

Token Maya Patel flew to New York .
Tag B-PER I-PER O O B-LOC I-LOC O

Why not just PER and LOC? Because two entities of the same type can sit side by side. In "gave Maria Lopez Garcia's notes", B tags are the only way to say whether that's one person or two. The model trained on these tags predicts one of 9 labels for each token: O, plus B- and I- for each of the four types.

Turning tags back into entities is a small state machine. Step through it and watch current grow and get flushed:

A B tag always starts a new entity, even right after another one. An O closes whatever was open. The final if current after the loop catches an entity that runs to the last token; forgetting it is the classic bug in this code, and it silently drops entities at the end of a sentence.

#Rules still win for some entities

The model knows four labels, so it has nothing to say about dates, prices, or email addresses. Run it on "Contact priya.shah@example.org about the Nov 3 invoice for $1,250 before 15 December 2026." and it returns an empty list. For entities with a regular shape, a few regular expressions do the job reliably:

re.finditer gives each match's start and end positions, the same character offsets the model reports, so rule and model results can be merged later. Rules are precise and explainable, but brittle: this month pattern also matches the start of Mayor or Marching when a number follows, and it knows nothing about next Tuesday. Real systems combine both, which is the next lesson's build.

#What the pipeline gives back

The pipeline's raw output is one dict per subword token, with its BIO label. The aggregation_strategy setting decides how those are grouped into entities. Run this in Colab:

Safaricom is split into three WordPiece tokens, and the model tagged each piece B-ORG instead of B-ORG, I-ORG, I-ORG. The simple strategy follows the BIO rules literally, so every B starts a new entity, and one company becomes three. The first strategy works at the word level: it gives the whole word the label of its first piece. That's why this course uses first (max and average are also word-level). O tokens are filtered out, and 5 March is missing because DATE isn't one of the model's labels.

#Inside the pipeline: from tokens to labels

The pipeline is three steps you can run yourself. The tokenizer makes ids, the model turns them into logits (one raw score per label per token), and a softmax turns each token's scores into probabilities:

The logits have shape [1, 8, 9]: one sentence, 8 tokens, 9 labels. model.config.id2label maps each label position to its name. torch.no_grad() tells PyTorch not to record the calculation for training, which saves memory when you only want predictions.

#What the transformer layers add: context

The box in the middle of that diagram is where context happens. Each token starts as a vector looked up from a table (plus a vector for its position), so Washington starts the same in every sentence. Each of the 6 layers then does two things:

  • Attention. Every token computes a weight for every token in the sentence, weights that are positive and add up to 1, and takes that weighted average of their vectors. Each layer has 12 heads that compute separate sets of weights, so one head can track the previous word while another tracks something else.
  • Feed-forward. Each token's vector goes through a small neural network on its own.

After 6 rounds, each token's vector depends on the whole sentence. You can measure it. Here's bank in three sentences, compared before the first layer and after the last:

Before any layer runs, the three bank vectors are nearly identical (they differ only by position). After six layers, the two river banks are still close and the money bank has moved away. That's the fix for the static-embedding problem from Module 2, and it's also how Jordan the person and Jordan the country end up with different labels. Module 5 looks at attention itself in detail.

#Common mistakes

⚠️ Watch out

Lowercasing before a cased model. The model reads capital letters as strong evidence. Lowercase the Module 1 sentence and run it again:

The person and the company vanish. Keep the original text for NER, even if you normalize a copy for search.

⚠️ Watch out

Reading the score as a guarantee. A score of 0.968 for the wrong label on Washington shows the score is the model's confidence, not a probability that it's right. Measure accuracy on labelled examples like your real text (the next two lessons do) before trusting any threshold.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What are the correct BIO tags for "Ana met Tom Lee in Rome"?

  • Ana is a one-token person, Tom Lee is a two-token person, and Rome is a location.

  • Two B tags in a row would make Tom and Lee two separate people.

  • Without B and I, adjacent entities of the same type can't be separated.

Show answer

A. Ana is a one-token person, Tom Lee is a two-token person, and Rome is a location.

2The BIO decoder in the trace forgets the final if current: entities.append(current). What breaks?

  • The loop only appends when the next B or O arrives.

  • With nothing after it to trigger the append, current is never saved.

  • The first entity is appended when the next B or O arrives.

Show answer

B. With nothing after it to trigger the append, current is never saved.

3The model tags Sa, ##fari, ##com as B-ORG, B-ORG, B-ORG. Which aggregation strategy returns one ORG entity, Safaricom?

  • That returns the three pieces separately, with their BIO tags.

  • It starts a new entity at every B tag, so it returns three.

  • Word-level strategies label each whole word, here using its first piece's label.

Show answer

C. Word-level strategies label each whole word, here using its first piece's label.

4The logits for a sentence have shape [1, 12, 9]. What does the 12 count?

  • It counts tokens, which can be more than words because of subword pieces and the special tokens.

  • One row of 9 label scores per token the model saw.

  • The heads live inside the layers; the classifier outputs one score per label per token.

Show answer

B. One row of 9 label scores per token the model saw.

Key takeaways

  • NER labels every token. BIO tags (B-, I-, O) let you recover spans and keep neighbouring entities apart.
  • Decoding BIO is a small state machine; don't forget the entity still open at the end.
  • A model only knows its training labels. Rules handle regular shapes like dates, money, and emails, and report the same character offsets.
  • Subword tokens can carry inconsistent tags. Word-level aggregation (first, max, average) keeps words whole.
  • Inside the pipeline: ids → embeddings → 6 layers of attention and feed-forward → logits of shape tokens × labels → softmax → labels.
  • Attention mixes context into every vector, so the same word gets different vectors (and labels) in different sentences.

#Further reading

  • Hugging Face LLM Course: Token classification (opens in a new tab): fine-tuning a model for NER, including how labels are aligned with subword tokens.
  • Hugging Face docs: Pipelines (opens in a new tab): every option of TokenClassificationPipeline, including the aggregation strategies.
  • The Illustrated Transformer, by Jay Alammar (opens in a new tab): the classic visual walk-through of attention and transformer layers.

m4-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write gold-standard entity labels as character spans, and score any extractor against them with span-level precision, recall, and F1.
  • Build a regex extractor for dates, money, and emails that reports the same span format as the model.
  • Merge rule and model entities so that each source covers what it's good at, without overlaps.
  • Read a model's per-token probabilities to understand one of its mistakes.
  • Pull attention weights out of a transformer and plot them as heatmaps.

Here is what you'll build, running on a sentence it has never seen:

Three entities come from regular expressions, two from the transformer, and the last column says which. Before writing it, you'll measure each half on hand-labelled text, so the claim "the combination is better" comes with numbers.

Make a notebook called nlp-m4-l2-entities.ipynb. Steps 1 to 4 run anywhere; the cells that load the model are marked for Colab.

#Step 1: Hand-label a small gold standard

Evaluation needs correct answers. Four short documents, with every entity written as (document, start, end, label). Typing character offsets by hand invites off-by-one errors, so a helper finds them with str.index:

Labelling forces decisions. Lagos Tech Summit is an event, so it's MISC, and the whole three words form the entity. Dr. is a title, not part of the name. Write these rules down when you label real data; two people labelling the same text disagree more often than you'd expect.

#Step 2: Score with exact span matching

A predicted entity counts as correct only if its document, start, end, and label all match a gold entity. With predictions and gold as sets of tuples, the matches are just their intersection:

Exact matching is strict on purpose. An extractor that finds Okafor instead of Amara Okafor gets no credit, because a redaction tool built on it would leave the first name visible.

#Step 3: The rule-based half

Three patterns, each producing spans in the same format. Order matters inside the DATE pattern: the longest forms come first, and a bare month name comes last so June on its own is still caught.

Precision 1.00, recall 0.50: everything the rules find is right, and they find exactly the half of the gold set that has a regular shape. The bare-month alternative is the risky one. It would also tag May in "May I ask a question?", so on real text you'd want it only after words like in or by.

#Step 4: The model half

Run this in Colab. It repeats the four documents so it works in a fresh session, and prints the model's entities as tuples you can copy:

Here's its output, pasted into a cell as data so the rest of the lesson runs anywhere:

The model's one real failure is Lagos Tech Summit: it split the event into a location and a shorter MISC, so the gold span and both predicted spans all count as errors. Notice its two lowest scores, 0.728 and 0.659, are exactly those two wrong entities. Low confidence doesn't always mean wrong, but here it would have been a useful warning.

#Step 5: Merge the two halves

The two halves cover different labels, so they mostly don't collide. When they do (say, the model tags riverbank inside an email address as an organization), the rule wins, because its patterns are more precise. The merge keeps every rule span, then adds each model span that doesn't overlap one:

Two spans overlap when each one starts before the other ends; that one-line test covers every case, including one span inside another. The per-label breakdown shows where the remaining errors live: all in MISC and LOC, both from the summit.

#Step 6: Look inside a wrong answer

The Notes lesson ended with a mistake: Washington signed the treaty in Washington gets LOC twice. Ask the model for its two best labels on every token (Colab):

PER was the model's second choice for the first Washington, at 0.025. It wasn't torn between the two; it was nearly certain and wrong. A plausible reason is the training data: in news text, Washington at the start of a sentence usually means the US government or the city, so signed wasn't enough evidence to override that. That's a guess about the data, not something the probabilities prove.

Two details in the code matter. attn_implementation="eager" loads the plain attention code, which can return its weights; the faster default implementation may not. output_attentions=True asks for them.

#Step 7: Chart what two attention heads look at

The model returns one attention tensor per layer, each shaped (batch, heads, tokens, tokens). Row i of a head's matrix holds the weights token i gives to every token, and each row adds up to 1:

Numbers like these are easier to read as pictures. Paste them into a plotting cell:

The left head does one simple job: almost every token puts nearly all its weight on the token just before it (the looks at signed, Washington looks at in). Heads like this let information flow from left to right through the sentence. The right panel looks nothing like a reading of the sentence: in the last layer, every token sends between a quarter and three quarters of its attention to [SEP]. Researchers have found this pattern in BERT-style models and read it as a "no-op": a head with nothing useful to collect parks its weight on a token that changes little.

That's the caution to carry into Module 5. Attention weights show where information could flow, not why the model chose a label. The first Washington gives most of its last-layer attention to [SEP], which tells you almost nothing about the mistake.

#The finished extractor

The whole thing as one Colab cell, ready to reuse. It repeats the rules so it runs on its own.

min_score drops model entities below a confidence threshold. At 0.7, the summit's MISC fragment (0.659) would have been dropped, which helps precision on this data; choose the value by scoring a labelled set, as in Step 5.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1The model predicts Okafor (PER) where the gold span is Amara Okafor (PER). How does exact span matching score it?

  • Exact matching has no partial credit.

  • The predicted span doesn't equal the gold span, so it lowers both precision and recall.

  • Start and end must match too.

Show answer

B. The predicted span doesn't equal the gold span, so it lowers both precision and recall.

2Why does the merge give rule spans priority over overlapping model spans?

  • Not always, but the rules' patterns are precise for the shapes they target.

  • Priority goes to the source you've measured to be more precise for that kind of span.

  • Sets hold any distinct tuples; overlap is about character ranges, which the set knows nothing about.

Show answer

B. Priority goes to the source you've measured to be more precise for that kind of span.

3The last layer's attention for the first Washington puts 0.70 on [SEP]. What can you conclude about its LOC label?

  • High attention to a separator token is a common pattern that carries little information.

  • Explaining a prediction needs other tools, such as testing how the output changes when you edit the input.

  • Earlier layers and other heads could still have carried information from signed.

Show answer

B. Explaining a prediction needs other tools, such as testing how the output changes when you edit the input.

Key takeaways

  • Gold labels as (doc, start, end, label) tuples make evaluation a set intersection. Exact matching gives no partial credit, which is what tasks like redaction need.
  • Rules and models fail differently: here, rules had perfect precision on half the labels and the model covered the other half. Measure each before combining.
  • Merge by priority: keep the more precise source's spans, and add the other's only where they don't overlap.
  • logits.softmax(-1) with topk shows how sure the model was and what it nearly chose.
  • With attn_implementation="eager" and output_attentions=True, attention comes back as one (batch, heads, tokens, tokens) tensor per layer, with rows that sum to 1.
  • Some heads have clear jobs, like attending to the previous token; many weights pile onto [SEP]. Attention is not an explanation.

What you'll learn

  • Decode BIO tags into spans, including the broken sequences real models produce.
  • Convert character-offset entities into BIO tags for a tokenized sentence.
  • Align word-level labels with subword tokens using word_ids, as NER fine-tuning requires.
  • Explain why token accuracy overstates NER quality, using span-level F1.
  • Turn a matrix of logits into word-level entities.
  • Compute attention weights with a softmax, and see what a causal mask changes.

All of these run without downloading anything. The subword tokens and word_ids in Exercises 3 and 5 are the real output of the course's tokenizer, copied in so you can work offline. Exercise 4 reuses the decoder you write in Exercise 1, so do them in order.

#Warm-up: tag a sentence

Replace the "O" placeholders in my_tags with the right BIO tags, then run the cell. Dr. is a title, not part of the name, and the BBC is an organization.

Each tuple is a token, your tag, and the right tag. With all placeholders left as "O", the five entity tokens show up as mistakes, while the six O tokens are already right: a reminder of why counting correct tags is a weak score, which Exercise 4 returns to.

#Exercise 1: Decode BIO tags, even broken ones

Write bio_to_spans(tags) that returns (label, start, end) tuples with end exclusive, like Python slices. Real models produce invalid sequences, so handle them the way the standard CoNLL scorer does: an I- tag that doesn't continue an entity of the same type starts a new entity.

Need a hint?

tag.partition("-") splits "I-PER" into ("I", "-", "PER") and "O" into ("O", "", ""). Track the open entity's label and start. At each tag, first decide whether it continues the open entity (an I- of the same type); if not, close the open one. Then decide whether this tag opens a new one. Appending an extra "O" to the tags closes anything still open at the end.

Show solution

The appended "O" replaces the "don't forget the last entity" check from the Notes trace: the loop always ends on an O, so whatever is open gets closed. The second line shows the repair rules at work. I-PER after O starts a person, and I-ORG after a B-LOC starts an organization instead of extending the location.

#Exercise 2: From character offsets to BIO tags

Labelling tools usually save entities as character offsets. Training needs one tag per token. Write char_spans_to_bio(text, entities) that tokenizes with re.finditer(r"\w+|[^\w\s]", text) and tags each token from (start, end, label) entities.

Need a hint?

A token belongs to an entity when it lies entirely inside it: start <= m.start() and m.end() <= end. It gets B- if it starts exactly where the entity starts, I- otherwise.

Show solution

If an entity boundary falls inside a token (say an annotator marked York in Yorkshire), no token fits entirely inside it and the entity silently disappears. Production code should count those cases and report them, since they usually mean the offsets and the tokenizer disagree.

#Exercise 3: Align word labels with subword tokens

You have one label per word, but the model predicts one label per subword token. Here is the real tokenizer output for "Kofi Mensah joined Safaricom in Nairobi .", passed in as a list of words:

Write align(word_ids, word_labels, every_piece=False) that returns one label id per token. Special tokens get -100, which PyTorch's loss function skips. The first piece of each word gets the word's label. Other pieces get -100 by default, or, with every_piece=True, the word's label with B- changed to I-.

Need a hint?

word_ids tells you which word each token came from (None for special tokens). A token starts a new word when its word id differs from the previous token's.

Show solution

Both conventions are in use; the Hugging Face course uses the second. Either way, ##fari must not get B-ORG, or the model learns that a company name starts in the middle of a word. A model trained without that care is exactly how you get the three-part Safaricom from the Notes lesson.

To produce word_ids yourself in Colab, call tokenizer(words, is_split_into_words=True).word_ids().

#Exercise 4: Token accuracy flatters NER

For "Maria del Carmen joined the World Bank in Lima .", a model predicts the tags below. Compute token-level accuracy, then span-level precision, recall, and F1 using bio_to_spans from Exercise 1.

Need a hint?

Turn both span lists into sets; the correct spans are their intersection, exactly as in the build-along.

Show solution

Two wrong tags out of ten look like 80% accuracy, but they turned one person into two fragments: one missed entity and two false ones. In real text, 80 to 90% of tokens are usually O, so a model that predicts O everywhere already scores high token accuracy while finding nothing. That's why NER papers report span-level F1, computed by tools like seqeval.

#Exercise 5: From logits to entities

The cell below simulates logits for the Exercise 3 tokens (random numbers with a boost on a planned label, since real logits need the model). One planned label is deliberately inconsistent: ##fari leans toward B-ORG. Apply a softmax, take each token's best label, keep the label of each word's first piece (the first aggregation strategy), and decode the word labels into entities.

Need a hint?

Softmax each row: np.exp(logits) / np.exp(logits).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True). Then walk word_ids alongside the token labels, keeping a label only when the word id is not None and differs from the previous one.

Show solution

At the token level, Safaricom is B-ORG, B-ORG, I-ORG, which simple aggregation would split in two. Taking only the first piece's label gives one clean word-level B-ORG. Softmax doesn't change which label is largest, so for picking labels the argmax of the logits gives the same answer; you need the probabilities only for the confidence score.

#Exercise 6: Attention weights, with and without a causal mask

Attention scores are turned into weights with a softmax along each row. Given these made-up scores for four tokens, compute the weights, check that every row sums to 1, and print which token each token attends to most. Then apply a causal mask, the one GPT-style models use so a token can't look at later tokens: set every score above the diagonal to minus infinity before the softmax.

Need a hint?

Subtract each row's maximum before np.exp so large scores can't overflow; it doesn't change the result. np.triu(np.ones((4, 4), dtype=bool), k=1) marks the positions above the diagonal, and np.where(mask, -np.inf, scores) applies the mask. exp(-inf) is exactly 0.

Show solution

With the mask, the can only look at itself, so its row becomes [1, 0, 0, 0], and every row's weight is redistributed over earlier tokens only. The last row is unchanged, because down is last and had no future to hide. The NER model in this course is an encoder with no mask, which is why its tokens can use words on both sides; Module 5 picks up from here.

#Challenge: A tested redaction tool

Write redact(text, model_spans) that replaces people, emails, and phone numbers with [PERSON], [EMAIL], and [PHONE], and leaves everything else alone. Emails and phone numbers (pattern \b\d{3}-\d{4}\b) come from regex rules; people come from the model, given as (start, end, label) spans. A rule span beats any overlapping model span. Test it with unittest, including a made-up model span that overlaps an email. The model spans for this sentence are the real output of the course's model:

Need a hint?

Replacing a span changes the length of the text, which shifts every offset after it. Replace from the end of the text backwards (sorted(spans, reverse=True)), and earlier offsets stay valid. Print test results to the output with unittest.TextTestRunner(stream=sys.stdout, verbosity=2).

Show solution

Without the overlap check, the second test replaces lima first, then cuts the email's original character range out of text that has already changed length, leaving a stray .net behind. Redaction is a task where recall matters more than precision: a missed name leaks, while an extra placeholder only costs some readability. The model scored Ana Lima at 0.831, the lowest score in its output; a real tool would log low-confidence spans for a person to check rather than trusting the threshold.

What you'll learn

  • Explain queries, keys, and values in plain words, then compute softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V in NumPy.
  • Read an attention heatmap: which token looks at which, and how much.
  • Show why the scores are divided by √d, and apply a causal mask before the softmax.
  • Explain why attention needs positional information, and why cost grows with the square of the context length.

Take two sentences: "deposit cash at the bank" and "the river bank flooded." The word embeddings you used in Module 2 give bank exactly one vector, the same in both. That vector has to sit halfway between money and water, which is right for neither sentence.

A transformer fixes this in one move. Before bank is passed on, it looks at the other words in its sentence and mixes some of their information into its own vector. Next to cash, it drifts toward money. Next to river, it drifts toward water. That mixing step is attention, and by the end of this page you'll have computed it with your own hands.

#Queries, keys, and values: a soft lookup

Here's the intuition. Every token does three jobs at once:

  • It sends out a query: "here's what I'm looking for."
  • It advertises a key: "here's what I contain, if you're looking."
  • It carries a value: "here's what I'll hand over if you pick me."

Each query is compared with every key. Close matches earn big scores, the scores become weights that add up to 1, and the token's new vector is the weighted blend of everyone's values. Think of a library search that hands you a blend of the books whose labels matched, mostly the best match.

Now precisely. Stack the tokens' vectors as rows of a matrix X (n tokens × d numbers). Three learned matrices turn it into Q = X·W_q, K = X·W_k, V = X·W_v. Then:

Q·Kᵀ is an n × n table of scores: row i, column j says how well token i's query matches token j's key. The softmax runs along each row, so every row of weights sums to 1.

Let's see it in code. I hand-built 4-number embeddings whose columns mean money, water, action, and filler word, so you can read the results. A trained model learns its W matrices; here they're identity matrices, so the query, key, and value of each token are just its embedding.

Look at the weights row. bank splits most of its attention between itself and river (0.36 each), gives a quarter to flooded, which has some water in it, and almost nothing to the. Its output vector went in as 1.5 money and 1.5 water and came out as 0.54 money and 2.23 water: the sentence pulled it toward the river meaning.

Before you run the next cell, predict: in "deposit cash at the bank", will bank end up higher in money or in water?

Same input vector for bank, two different outputs. A real model does this with hundreds of dimensions, dozens of layers, and many attention heads per layer, each with its own learned W matrices.

#Reading an attention heatmap

The weights matrix is easier to read as a picture. Each row is one token's query, and the colors across it show where its attention goes.

The three content words form a block in the lower right: they share the water dimension, so their queries and keys match, and the column for the is nearly white below the first row. the matches nothing but itself, keeps 0.71 of its weight, and spreads the rest evenly. Heatmaps from trained models are messier, but you read them the same way.

#Why divide by √d

Leave out the / np.sqrt(d) and the code still runs; the trouble shows up in wide models. A dot product of two d-dimensional vectors with random unit-sized entries has a spread of about √d, so at d = 512 raw scores swing by ±20. Softmax of numbers that far apart is nearly one-hot, and training gets tiny gradients for every other token.

With 8 keys, a fair spread would give the top key around 0.3. Unscaled, the top key's share climbs to 0.95 as d grows. Scaled, it stays near 0.36 for every size. Dividing by √d keeps the softmax in a range where learning works, whatever the model's width.

#Masking: a GPT-style model can't read ahead

A model that writes one token at a time is trained to predict each next token. If position 3 could attend to position 4, it would just copy the answer. So decoder models like GPT apply a causal mask: before the softmax, every score where the key comes after the query becomes −∞. Since e^(−∞) = 0, those weights are exactly zero and the rest still sum to 1.

Step through one row. Token 1 (the second token) is allowed to see tokens 0 and 1, but not token 2:

Notice that the 3.0 was the largest score, and it ends up with weight 0. In NumPy, the whole matrix gets masked at once with np.triu:

The first row is [1, 0, 0, 0]: the first token can only look at itself, and each later row spreads over one more token. BERT-style encoders skip this mask, so they read whole sentences well but don't generate text left to right.

#Attention can't see word order on its own

Shuffle the rows of X and attention shuffles its output rows the same way, but each token's output vector doesn't change. To attention, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" are the same bag of tokens.

Without positions, dog gets the identical vector whether it's biting or bitten. Adding a position signal breaks the tie. The original transformer added the sine and cosine waves used here, GPT-2 learned one vector per position, and many current models (Llama among them) rotate queries and keys by a position-dependent angle, called RoPE.

#A context window is a budget, and it's measured in tokens

Every query is scored against every key, so n tokens produce n × n scores, in every head of every layer.

That square growth is one reason every model has a context window, a maximum number of tokens per call. The window holds everything: instructions, chat history, pasted documents, your question, and the answer the model writes. Tokens aren't words, either. For English prose, a rule of thumb many providers quote is about 4 characters per token; code, numbers, and many other languages need more.

What happens at the limit depends on the tool. Many APIs reject an over-long request with an error, which is easy to notice. Hugging Face tokenizers called with truncation=True quietly cut tokens off the end. Chat apps often drop the oldest messages, so the definitions you pasted first are the first to go.

Even when everything fits, position matters: in the 2023 "Lost in the Middle" study, models used a fact best when it sat near the start or end of a long context. Next lesson you'll build a planner that decides what goes into the window instead of letting truncation decide.

⚠️ Watch out

Softmax over the wrong axis. Normalizing with axis=0 makes each column sum to 1 instead of each query's row. The code runs, the shapes are right, and the output is wrong. Check that weights.sum(axis=1) is all ones.

Masking after the softmax. Zeroing future weights after the softmax leaves rows that sum to less than 1, and the earlier weights were already shaped by the future scores. Mask the scores with −∞, then take the softmax.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A query's scores against three keys are [2.0, 2.0, 2.0]. What are its attention weights?

  • Softmax weights always sum to 1, so three equal weights can't each be 1.

  • Equal scores give equal weights, and they must sum to 1.

  • A one-hot result needs one score far above the others; these are tied.

Show answer

B. Equal scores give equal weights, and they must sum to 1.

2You remove / np.sqrt(d) from a model with d = 1024. What happens to the attention weights?

  • Softmax makes the weights sum to 1 but doesn't undo a large spread.

  • Raw scores have a spread near √1024 = 32, so the softmax saturates.

  • Near-uniform weights come from scores close together, the opposite of what removing the scale does.

Show answer

B. Raw scores have a spread near √1024 = 32, so the softmax saturates.

3In a causal (GPT-style) model, which keys can token 4 (counting from 0) attend to?

  • That's an encoder like BERT, with no mask.

  • The mask hides keys after the query's own position; the token can see itself and everything before it.

  • Attention isn't limited to the previous token; it blends all visible tokens.

Show answer

B. The mask hides keys after the query's own position; the token can see itself and everything before it.

4A chatbot that keeps the latest messages and drops old ones starts ignoring rules you gave at the start. What's the most likely cause?

  • Short text attends fine; length isn't the issue.

  • Chat tools often drop the oldest turns to stay under the limit, and your rules were the oldest turn.

  • Attention covers every token inside the window, however many messages that spans.

Show answer

B. Chat tools often drop the oldest turns to stay under the limit, and your rules were the oldest turn.

Key takeaways

  • softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V rebuilds each token as a blend of other tokens' values; each row of weights belongs to one query and sums to 1.
  • Dividing by √d keeps wide models from saturating the softmax.
  • A causal mask sets future scores to −∞ before the softmax, so a generating model can't peek ahead.
  • Attention alone ignores order; positional encodings put "where" into the vectors.
  • A context window caps input and output tokens together, and over-long text is often cut without warning.

#Further reading

  • Attention Is All You Need (opens in a new tab): the 2017 paper that introduced the transformer. Section 3.2 defines scaled dot-product attention in one page.
  • The Illustrated Transformer (opens in a new tab) by Jay Alammar: the same computation drawn as pictures, with every matrix shape labeled.
  • Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (opens in a new tab): the study showing that facts buried mid-context get used less.

What you'll learn

  • Estimate token counts with a simple tokenizer and know which direction it errs.
  • Split a context window into a budget: instructions, question, document, and room for the answer.
  • Show how keep-the-start and keep-the-end truncation each lose a different part of a document.
  • Build a planner that pins required sections, ranks the rest by relevance, packs them to fit, and reports every section it dropped.

A student asks the school's help bot: "Can a part-time student borrow a laptop over the summer?" The right answer needs two pieces of the lending policy: the definition of an eligible student near the top, and the summer rules near the bottom. The whole policy doesn't fit in the model's window, so something gets cut. If the cut happens wherever the tokens run out, the bot answers confidently from half the rules.

Here's what you'll build: a planner that takes the policy, the question, and a window size, and returns a prompt that fits plus a report like this one.

We'll pretend the model has a 512-token window (the limit of BERT-style models) so the numbers stay readable. Current chat models allow 128,000 tokens or more, but a stack of handbooks fills that just as surely, and the arithmetic doesn't change.

#Step 1: The document and the question

The policy is a dictionary of sections, title to text. Keeping the structure is the first decision: a section is a unit of meaning, while a random 300-token slice is not.

#Step 2: Estimate tokens

Exact counts need the model's own tokenizer, and every model family has a different one. For planning, an estimate is enough as long as you know which way it leans. This one splits text into words and punctuation marks, counts short words as one token, and charges long words about one token per four letters, because subword tokenizers break rare long words into pieces.

The two estimates agree within a few percent. When I ran this policy through real tokenizers (OpenAI's tiktoken with the GPT-2 and o200k_base encodings), they counted between 523 and 544 tokens for the policy, where this estimator says about 630, so it runs roughly 15 to 20 percent high. That's the safe direction: a budget built on an overestimate leaves spare room instead of overflowing.

📝 Note

For exact numbers in Colab, load the tokenizer of the model you'll actually call, such as AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2") from Hugging Face transformers, and count with len(tokenizer(text)["input_ids"]). Hosted APIs also report the true counts in each response's usage field.

#Step 3: Split the window into a budget

The window has to hold everything at once, and the answer is part of it. Forget to reserve room for the answer and the model gets cut off mid-sentence, or the API refuses the request.

Only about half of the policy fits. Now the question is which half.

#Step 4: Watch truncation drop the wrong part

The simplest fix is to cut the text when the tokens run out. Tools do this in two directions: tokenizers usually keep the start, and chat apps usually keep the most recent text, which is the end. Predict before you run: which section does each one lose that our question needs?

Keeping the start loses section 8, so the model never sees the summer rule. Keeping the end loses section 1, so the model reads "students without approved eligibility" without knowing that part-time students need a counselor's approval. Both prompts look fine, both answers can sound sure of themselves, and both cuts land mid-section. Nothing raised an error.

#Step 5: Pin, rank, and pack

A better planner makes three decisions on purpose:

  1. Pin what every answer depends on. Definitions change the meaning of every other section, so they always go in.
  2. Rank the rest by how much they share with the question. Here that's a plain word overlap; in Module 6 you'll swap in TF-IDF retrieval.
  3. Pack whole sections, best first, until the budget is full, and record every section that didn't make it.

The planner kept Definitions, Borrowing, Loan periods, and Summer loans: exactly the sections a person would read to answer this question. Two details matter. A section with zero overlap is dropped even if there's room, since unrelated text costs tokens and can distract the model. And if the pinned sections alone are too big, pack raises a ValueError instead of quietly cutting the definitions.

#Step 6: Build the prompt and check the bill

The chosen sections go back in their original order, so the excerpt reads like the policy. The prompt also tells the model what was left out, which gives it a fair way to say "that isn't in the excerpt."

The assert is the line that turns "probably fits" into "checked." The chart compares this plan with pasting everything:

#The finished planner

Here is the planner as one function. It reuses estimate_tokens, format_section, pack, and build_prompt from the steps above; to save it as a script, paste those functions and the Step 1 data above it.

The second question swaps Summer loans out and Damage and loss in, from the same code. The planner works per question, which is the idea that retrieval-augmented generation scales up.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the planner reserve 100 tokens for the answer instead of giving all leftover space to the document?

  • The estimate leans high already; the reserve is for a different reason.

  • Input and output share the context window; with no reserve the answer can be cut short or the request rejected.

  • There's no such rule; the limit is the total of input and output tokens.

Show answer

B. Input and output share the context window; with no reserve the answer can be cut short or the request rejected.

2The policy grows, and Definitions alone now costs more than the document budget. What does pack do?

  • That would recreate the silent-loss problem the planner exists to stop.

  • Pinned sections are never skipped; the answers depend on them.

  • Failing loudly forces a human decision: a bigger window, shorter definitions, or splitting the task.

Show answer

C. Failing loudly forces a human decision: a bigger window, shorter definitions, or splitting the task.

3Why does the prompt list the omitted section numbers?

  • A model told what's missing has an honest way to say "not in the provided excerpt."

  • A plain chat model can't fetch anything; it only reads the prompt.

  • Extra tokens are a cost, not a benefit; the list is there for honesty about coverage.

Show answer

A. A model told what's missing has an honest way to say "not in the provided excerpt."

Key takeaways

  • Estimate tokens with a method that leans high, and check it against a real tokenizer once.
  • A context budget is window = instructions + question + document + answer reserve.
  • Truncation cuts wherever tokens run out, often mid-section, with no warning; which end it keeps decides what you lose.
  • Pin what every answer depends on, rank the rest against the question, pack whole sections, and report what you dropped.
  • Fail loudly when the pinned content alone won't fit.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Pack by value per token: divide relevance by cost so short, relevant sections beat long, slightly relevant ones.
  • Split oversized sections into paragraphs before packing, keeping the section title on each piece.
  • Add a "keep the last N chat turns" mode and check that a pinned rule survives a long conversation.

#Further reading

  • Padding and truncation (opens in a new tab) in the Hugging Face docs: what truncation=True and max_length actually do, and which side gets cut.
  • tiktoken (opens in a new tab): OpenAI's tokenizer library, for exact counts with GPT encodings in Colab.
  • Long context prompting (opens in a new tab) in Anthropic's prompting guide: where to put long documents in a prompt and how to ask about them.

What you'll learn

  • Write a numerically stable softmax and explain why subtracting the maximum is safe.
  • Compute attention weights from Q and K and say which token each one attends to.
  • Build a causal mask and split attention into heads.
  • Budget a chat history with a pinned message, and order chunks to avoid the middle of a long context.

#Warm-up: predict three softmaxes

Before running anything, guess: what is softmax([1, 2, 3])? Will softmax([2, 4, 6]) be flatter or sharper? And what about softmax([101, 102, 103])?

Doubling the scores sharpens the weights, because softmax cares about the gaps between scores. Adding 100 to every score changes nothing at all: only differences matter. That second fact is what makes Exercise 1 work.

#Exercise 1: A softmax that doesn't overflow

The textbook formula, exp(x) / sum(exp(x)), breaks on large scores. Run this and look at the result:

np.exp(1000) is larger than the biggest float, so it becomes inf, and inf / inf is nan. Write stable_softmax(x) that works on a 2-D array of scores, one row per query, and returns rows that each sum to 1. Test it on [[1000, 1001, 1002], [1, 2, 3]].

Need a hint?

The warm-up showed that subtracting the same number from every score in a row leaves the softmax unchanged. Which number would make the biggest exponent exactly exp(0) = 1? Use keepdims=True so the subtraction lines up row by row.

Show solution

After subtracting each row's maximum, the largest exponent is exp(0) = 1 and the rest are smaller, so nothing overflows. Both rows give the same weights because they have the same gaps. Every deep learning library's softmax does this shift internally.

#Exercise 2: Who attends to whom?

Here are queries and keys for the sentence "she fed her cat", with d = 2. Compute the attention weights softmax(QKᵀ/√d) and, for each token, print the token it attends to most and that weight.

Need a hint?

Q @ K.T gives a 4 × 4 score table. Divide by np.sqrt(2), softmax each row, then use .argmax() on each row to find the column with the biggest weight.

Show solution

I chose these vectors so the pattern reads like grammar: her looks back at she, and the verb fed looks at its object cat. In a trained model, heads that track pronouns or verb objects like this do turn up, though most heads are far harder to name.

#Exercise 3: Build and test a causal mask

For n = 5 tokens with random scores (np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal((5, 5))), apply a causal mask and softmax. Then check three things in code: every row sums to 1, every weight above the diagonal is exactly 0, and the count of visible (query, key) pairs is 15 of 25.

Need a hint?

np.triu(np.ones((n, n), dtype=bool), k=1) is True exactly where the key is in the future. Put -np.inf there with np.where before the softmax. For the visible count, n(n + 1)/2 is the formula to check against.

Show solution

weights[future] picks out every entry above the diagonal using the same boolean mask, so one line checks all ten of them. A generating model needs only the lower triangle, about half the scores, but the cost still grows with n².

#Exercise 4: Two heads instead of one

Real layers run several attention heads side by side, each on its own slice of the vectors. With rng = np.random.default_rng(42), make X of shape (4, 6) and three (6, 6) weight matrices. Compute Q, K, V, split their 6 columns into 2 heads of 3, run attention in each head (scale by √3), print token 0's weights in each head, and concatenate the head outputs back to shape (4, 6).

Need a hint?

Head h uses columns h * 3 to h * 3 + 3. Slice Q[:, cols], K[:, cols], and V[:, cols] with the same cols, and join the results with np.concatenate(outputs, axis=1). Make the matrices in the order X, W_q, W_k, W_v so your random numbers match.

Show solution

Same token, two very different patterns: head 0 sends token 0's attention to token 3, while head 1 keeps most of it on token 0 itself. That's why models use many heads: each can track a different relationship at the same cost as one wide head. Real layers then multiply the concatenated output by one more learned matrix.

#Exercise 5: Budget a long chat

A chat model has a 4,096-token window. The system prompt costs 350 tokens, and you reserve 800 for the reply. Message 0 contains the user's rules for the whole conversation, so it is pinned. The other messages must be kept as a contiguous run of the most recent ones: walk backward from the newest and stop at the first message that doesn't fit.

Need a hint?

Start the budget at 4096 − 350 − 800 − 420. Loop for i in range(len(messages) - 1, 0, -1), and break (not continue) when a message is too big, so you never keep message 3 while skipping message 4.

Show solution

Message 4, at 1,200 tokens, is the one that doesn't fit, so it and everything older (except the pinned rules) is dropped. Using continue would sneak message 3 back in and leave a gap the model can't see, which makes the conversation read as if a turn never happened. About 1,100 tokens go unused; a fancier planner could summarize messages 1 to 4 into that space.

#Exercise 6: Keep key chunks out of the middle

Long-context studies found that models use information at the start and end of the context better than information in the middle. Given chunks already ranked best-first, write edges_first(ranked) that places the best chunk first, the second-best last, the third second, the fourth second-to-last, and so on, so the weakest chunks end up in the middle.

Need a hint?

Every other chunk, starting with the best, goes on the front in order: ranked[0::2]. The rest go on the back, reversed so the second-best ends up last.

Show solution

With six chunks, the best two (A and B) sit at the very edges and the weakest (F and E) meet in the middle. This is a cheap fix to try, and you should measure it on your own questions: newer models are better at long contexts, and the effect varies by model.

#Challenge: Positional encodings that know distance

Implement the sinusoidal encoding from the original transformer: for position pos and dimension i, use sin(pos / 10000^(2⌊i/2⌋/d)) on even i and cos of the same angle on odd i. Build the matrix for 50 positions and d = 16, draw it as a heatmap, and then show that the dot product PE[p] · PE[p + k] depends only on the offset k, not on the starting position p. Print it for p in 0, 10, 25 and k in 0, 1, 5, 20.

Need a hint?

Broadcasting does the work: pos = np.arange(50)[:, None] and i = np.arange(16)[None, :] give a 50 × 16 grid of angles. For the dot products, PE[p] @ PE[p + k] is one number per (p, k) pair.

Show solution

The three rows of numbers are identical. Each sine and cosine pair contributes sin(a·p)sin(a·(p+k)) + cos(a·p)cos(a·(p+k)) = cos(a·k), and p cancels out. So two tokens five apart have the same positional similarity anywhere in the sentence, which helps a model learn patterns like "the word two to the left" once instead of separately for every position.

What you'll learn

  • Build a chat prompt from a template: system rules, delimited sources, few-shot examples, and the question.
  • Write a JSON Schema and a Pydantic model for a model's answer, and read the validation errors.
  • Explain retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): chunk, index, retrieve, then prompt.
  • Check that every citation in an answer points at a source that was actually retrieved.

You ask a model to answer from the lending policy and reply with JSON containing answer, citations, and answerable. This comes back:

Count the failures. There's chatter before the JSON, so a parser chokes. The key is Answer, not answer. The answerable field is missing. The citation names a handbook page nobody retrieved. And the answer is wrong: part-time students need a counselor's approval. Every one of these has a fix you can write in code: a better prompt, a schema, retrieval, and a citation check.

#A prompt has parts, so build it like code

Chat models take a list of messages, each with a role. The system message holds rules that apply to the whole conversation. user messages carry the task and the data. assistant messages are the model's replies, and you can write some yourself to show the model examples.

A reliable prompt usually has the same pieces: what the model is for, the rules, the context it may use, examples, the output format, and finally the input. Building it with a function means every request follows the same template, and you can test and version that template like any other code.

The <source id="..."> tags matter more than they look. They separate your instructions from document text, give each source an id the model can cite, and make it harder for a sentence inside a document to pass itself off as an instruction. Any clear delimiter works; XML-style tags are a common choice because models have seen many of them.

#Few-shot examples teach the format and the edge cases

A zero-shot prompt only describes what you want. A few-shot prompt also shows it: a handful of example inputs, each followed by the exact reply you'd want. Examples beat descriptions at pinning down format, and they're the best way to teach the case models get wrong most often, which here is admitting the sources don't say.

Two examples, one answerable and one not. If both were answerable, you'd be quietly teaching the model that the answer is always yes. Keep examples short, make them cover different cases, and don't reuse the real question's sources in them, or the model may copy an example's answer.

#A schema is a contract you can check

A JSON Schema says exactly what valid output looks like: which keys, which types, which are required, and whether extra keys are allowed. First, though, the reply has to parse:

"Expecting value: line 1 column 1" means the parser hit S where JSON should start. Cutting from the first { to the last } gets past the chatter, and then the schema reports every remaining problem at once:

Four errors covering three failures: the wrong key name (reported twice, as a missing answer and an unexpected Answer), the missing answerable, and a citation that isn't a source id. The extraction handled the chatter. The wrong answer sails through. In Python code, Pydantic expresses the same contract as a class, and validation gives you a typed object you can use with attribute access:

Many APIs can now enforce a schema while the model writes, called structured outputs: OpenAI's response_format with a JSON Schema, Gemini's response schema, and Ollama's format parameter. When it's supported, the reply always parses and has the right keys. Keep validating anyway: support for schema features varies by provider and model, and a perfectly shaped answer can still be false.

#Retrieval puts the facts in the prompt

A model only knows what was in its training data, which stops at a cutoff date and never included your school's policy. Retrieval-augmented generation fixes that at question time: find the passages most related to the question, put them in the prompt as numbered sources, and tell the model to answer only from them.

Chunking decides what the retriever can find. Split along the document's own structure (sections, then paragraphs) so each chunk is about one thing. Chunks that are too small lose context ("it must be returned within five days": what must?). Chunks that are too big mix topics, which blurs the match and spends your token budget. Many systems also let neighboring chunks overlap by a sentence or two so a fact that straddles a boundary survives whole. Retrieval can use the TF-IDF vectors you built in Module 2, dense embeddings, or both. Next lesson you'll build the TF-IDF version end to end.

#Citations you can verify

Retrieval gives you something prompting alone can't: a list of what the model was shown. That makes the invented-source failure checkable in one line.

A real id doesn't prove the source supports the sentence, only that it exists. Module 7 adds that second check.

#Sending it to a real model

This cell runs in Colab, not on this page. It uses the openai Python package, which also talks to Google's Gemini API (free tier) and to Ollama on your own computer, because both offer OpenAI-compatible endpoints.

📝 Note

One-time setup for Gemini. Create a key at Google AI Studio (opens in a new tab). In Colab, open Secrets (the key icon), add a secret named GEMINI_API_KEY, and switch on Notebook access. Using Ollama instead? Install it from ollama.com, run ollama pull llama3.2, and create the client with OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1/", api_key="ollama") and model="llama3.2". Model names change often, so check your provider's model list if one is rejected.

parse turns the Pydantic class into a JSON Schema, sends it as the response format, and hands back a validated GroundedAnswer. Text you send to a hosted API leaves your computer, so use only non-sensitive documents with it.

⚠️ Watch out

Calling json.loads on the raw reply. Models often wrap JSON in a sentence or in a Markdown code fence, and you get JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0). Use structured outputs when the API has them; otherwise extract from the first { to the last } and validate.

Treating "valid" as "correct." A schema checks shape. {"answer": "Yes", "citations": ["S1"], "answerable": true} passes every check on this page and is still the wrong answer to the summer question.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Your few-shot prompt has four examples, and all four are answerable questions with "yes" answers. What risk does that add?

  • Four short examples cost little; the problem is what they teach.

  • Examples teach patterns, including accidental ones. Cover the unanswerable case on purpose.

  • Nothing in these examples models a refusal; if anything they push the other way.

Show answer

B. Examples teach patterns, including accidental ones. Cover the unanswerable case on purpose.

2Which problem in a reply would a JSON Schema with "required" and "additionalProperties": false catch?

  • answer is reported missing and Answer is reported as an unexpected extra key.

  • A schema checks structure and types, not whether the content is true.

  • S2 matches the pattern; checking support needs a different test.

Show answer

A. answer is reported missing and Answer is reported as an unexpected extra key.

3The retriever returned S1, S2, and S3. The reply cites ["S2", "S9"]. What should the system do?

  • One invented citation means you can't trust which claims came from where.

  • The model can only legitimately cite what it was shown; anything else is fabricated.

  • Ids are labels you assigned in this prompt; S9 doesn't refer to anything.

Show answer

B. The model can only legitimately cite what it was shown; anything else is fabricated.

4You split a policy into chunks of 15 words each. What is the most likely problem?

  • Small chunks are cheap; the trouble is what each one means on its own.

  • Tiny chunks cut facts away from the words that make them meaningful.

  • TF-IDF works on short text; it just has less to match on.

Show answer

B. Tiny chunks cut facts away from the words that make them meaningful.

Key takeaways

  • Build prompts with a function: system rules, delimited sources with ids, few-shot examples, then the question.
  • Few-shot examples should cover different cases, including the one where the sources don't answer.
  • Validate every reply against a schema (JSON Schema or Pydantic), even when the API enforces one.
  • RAG retrieves relevant chunks at question time and puts them in the prompt; chunking by structure decides what can be found.
  • Check that citations are a subset of what was retrieved. A schema-valid, well-cited answer can still be wrong, so test support next.

#Further reading

  • Structured outputs (opens in a new tab) in the OpenAI docs: how schema-constrained replies work, which schema features are supported, and how refusals are reported.
  • Understanding JSON Schema (opens in a new tab): a readable reference for every keyword used on this page.
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (opens in a new tab): the 2020 paper that named RAG.

m6-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Chunk documents along their structure, with a one-sentence overlap for long paragraphs.
  • Index the chunks with TF-IDF and retrieve the top matches for a question.
  • See what a similarity threshold can and can't catch.
  • Build a prompt with numbered sources, then validate replies with a strict Pydantic model and a citation check.

Here's the finished pipeline answering a question about a public library's rules. The "model" in this run is a stand-in that copies the source sentence that best matches the question, so everything works on this page with no API key. In Colab you swap in a real model with one argument.

Every answer comes back with the chunk ids it relied on, or with a reason it was rejected. Nothing reaches the user without passing the checks.

#Step 1: The documents

Six help pages for a made-up public library, each a title and some paragraphs. Blank lines separate the paragraphs, and we'll use that structure when we chunk.

#Step 2: Chunk along paragraphs, with overlap where needed

Each paragraph becomes a chunk. A paragraph longer than max_words is split into runs of whole sentences, and each run after the first starts with the last sentence of the one before, so a fact near a boundary appears whole in at least one chunk. Chunk ids like fees#1 record where every chunk came from.

Only the first fees paragraph was long enough to split. Look at the two chunks: the sentence about items 30 days overdue ends fees#0 and starts fees#1. Without that overlap, fees#1 would begin with "The bill is removed...", and a reader (or a model) couldn't tell which bill.

#Step 3: Index with TF-IDF and retrieve

TF-IDF from Module 2 scores words that are frequent in a chunk and rare across chunks. One problem shows up fast: "Can I renew a laptop?" shares no exact words with "Laptops and hotspots cannot be renewed." A small analyzer that drops stop words and trims -s, -ed, and -ing fixes most of that.

Two choices in that cell matter. Each chunk is indexed with its title in front, so "fees" questions match fee chunks even when the paragraph doesn't repeat the word. And retrieve returns scores along with ids, because the next step needs them.

#Step 4: Decide when retrieval found nothing

If the best chunk barely matches, there's no point asking a model; it can only guess. So set a floor on the top score. Before you look at the chart, predict: will the three questions this library can't answer all score below the five it can?

The World Cup question matches nothing and falls below the floor. But "Does the library rent bikes?" scores 0.29 because it shares library with the fees page, and the Sunday-hours question scores 0.43 by matching hours in the study-room rules, higher than the real grandmother question. Retrieval measures shared words, not whether a chunk answers the question. The floor stays low, and the prompt lets the model say answerable: false for the rest.

#Step 5: Build the grounded prompt

Each retrieved chunk is shown to the model as a numbered source: S1, S2, S3. Short ids are easy for a model to copy exactly, and id_map translates them back to real chunk ids afterward.

Notice S3, the accessibility chunk. It was retrieved because it shares book (from books), and it has nothing to do with study rooms. Retrieval always returns k chunks, relevant or not, which is one more reason the rules tell the model to use only what answers the question.

#Step 6: Parse and check every reply

The parser accepts a reply only if it contains a JSON object that passes a strict Pydantic model and cites only sources it was shown. Strict matters: by default Pydantic quietly converts the string "yes" to True, which hides a model that isn't following the format.

These four replies are written to match the shapes you'll meet from real models: clean JSON, JSON in a Markdown fence with a made-up source, plain prose, and the wrong types.

The fenced reply parses fine, since we cut from the first { to the last }, but it cites S4, and only S1 to S3 were shown. That's the invented-source failure from the start of this module, caught by one list comprehension.

#The finished pipeline

answer ties the steps together. The model call is a parameter, so the same function runs offline with a stand-in and in Colab with a real model.

The first two answers are right, and the World Cup question never reaches the model. Now look at the bikes question. The stand-in returns a sentence about late fines, cites a source it was really shown, and passes every check in parse_reply. A well-formed answer with a real citation can still have nothing to do with the question; checking that the cited source supports the answer is the job of Module 7. A real model would most likely say answerable: false here, which is one reason to plug one in. To use Gemini or Ollama in Colab, define call_model with the client from the last lesson:

temperature=0 makes replies as repeatable as the provider allows, which you'll want when you start measuring them in Module 7.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does each chunk get indexed as title + ". " + text instead of just the text?

  • TF-IDF works on short text; length isn't the reason.

  • "Rooms are released if no one checks in..." never says "study", but its title does.

  • Citations use the S ids; the title helps retrieval, not citation.

Show answer

B. "Rooms are released if no one checks in..." never says "study", but its title does.

2"What are the opening hours on Sunday?" retrieves a study-room chunk with a score of 0.43. Which part of the pipeline should handle it?

  • That would also reject real questions, like the grandmother one at 0.33.

  • Retrieval can't tell shared words from an answer; the prompt and schema give the model an honest way out.

  • The parser checks format and citations, not whether the answer is right.

Show answer

B. Retrieval can't tell shared words from an answer; the prompt and schema give the model an honest way out.

3Why does GroundedAnswer use strict=True?

  • Strict mode rejects type coercion, which exposes a model that isn't following the schema.

  • Pydantic only checks replies after they arrive; it can't control the model.

  • That's extra="forbid", a separate setting.

Show answer

A. Strict mode rejects type coercion, which exposes a model that isn't following the schema.

Key takeaways

  • Chunk by structure first, split only long paragraphs, and overlap by a sentence so boundary facts survive.
  • Index chunks with their titles, and keep chunk ids so every answer can point back to its source.
  • A score floor catches questions that match nothing; it can't catch questions that match the wrong words.
  • Show sources with short ids, map them back afterward, and reject any reply that cites an id you didn't show.
  • Pass the model call in as a function, so the whole pipeline can run and be tested offline.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Swap TF-IDF for sentence embeddings (the sentence-transformers library in Colab) and rerun Step 4's chart. Does the Sunday question still score above the grandmother one?
  • On a rejected reply, retry once with the problems appended to the prompt, then give up.
  • Combine scores from TF-IDF and embeddings (hybrid retrieval) and compare the top chunks.

#Further reading

  • TfidfVectorizer (opens in a new tab) in the scikit-learn docs: every option used here, including a custom analyzer.
  • Strict mode (opens in a new tab) in the Pydantic docs: exactly which conversions lax mode allows and strict mode refuses.
  • Advanced RAG on Hugging Face documentation (opens in a new tab) in the Hugging Face cookbook: the same pipeline with embeddings, a vector index, and a reranker.

m6-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Extract a JSON object from replies wrapped in fences or followed by chatter.
  • Express one output contract as a JSON Schema and as a Pydantic model, and compare their errors.
  • Pick few-shot examples that cover every label.
  • Chunk text with overlap, measure retrieval with hit@k, and spot prompt injection in retrieved text.

#Warm-up: which of these does json.loads accept?

Models trained on lots of Python sometimes write Python-flavored JSON. Predict which of these four strings parse, then run it.

Only the first one. JSON requires double quotes, lowercase true, and no trailing commas, and each error message tells you exactly which rule broke and at which character.

#Exercise 1: Pull JSON out of a messy reply

Write extract_json(text) that returns the first JSON object in a reply as a dict, or raises ValueError if there isn't one. It must handle all three replies below. The second is the trap: cutting from the first { to the last } grabs {smile} too.

Need a hint?

Check for a Markdown fence first with a regular expression. For the rest, json.JSONDecoder().raw_decode(text, start) parses one complete JSON value starting at index start and ignores whatever comes after it.

Show solution

raw_decode stops at the end of the first complete object, so trailing text, even text with braces in it, is ignored. JSONDecodeError is a subclass of ValueError, so the one except also catches a reply whose JSON is broken.

#Exercise 2: A schema for ticket triage

A support bot labels each message. Write TICKET_SCHEMA so that a valid output has exactly four keys: category (one of billing, bug, account, other), priority (a whole number from 1 to 5), summary (a string of at most 80 characters), and needs_human (true or false). Validate the three outputs below and print each error's path and the schema keyword that failed.

Need a hint?

enum lists allowed values; minimum, maximum, and maxLength set limits; required plus "additionalProperties": False pins down the keys. Each error from iter_errors has .json_path and .validator (the keyword that failed).

Show solution

"Billing" fails because enum compares exactly, capital letters included. Decide whether that's what you want: you might lowercase the category before validating, but you should never lowercase silently and forget you did it.

#Exercise 3: The same contract in Pydantic

Write a Ticket Pydantic model that enforces the same rules, in strict mode, and validate the same three outputs. For each failure, print how many errors there were and which fields they were on.

Need a hint?

Literal["billing", "bug", "account", "other"] restricts a string to those values. Field(ge=1, le=5) and Field(max_length=80) set limits. ConfigDict(extra="forbid", strict=True) handles extra keys and stops "yes" from becoming True.

Show solution

Same five errors as the JSON Schema version. The difference is what you get on success: a Ticket object with typed attributes, and Ticket.model_json_schema() will produce a JSON Schema you can send to an API's structured-output mode, so one class serves both jobs.

#Exercise 4: Few-shot examples that cover every label

You have a pool of labeled messages. Write pick_examples(pool, k) that takes examples round-robin across labels (in alphabetical label order), so 4 examples cover 4 labels and 6 examples go around a second time. Keep each label's examples in their pool order.

Need a hint?

Group the pool into a dict of label → list of examples. Then loop over rounds: in round r, take the r-th example of each label that has one, stopping when you have k.

Show solution

The pool has three examples each of billing, bug, and account, and only one "other". Taking the first four from the pool would give two billing, one bug, one account, and no "other" at all, and the model would rarely use a label it never saw. The took_any check stops the loop when the pool runs out, so asking for 20 examples returns 10 instead of looping forever.

#Exercise 5: Chunk by words with overlap

Write chunk_words(text, size, overlap) that returns lists of words: each chunk has size words and starts size − overlap words after the previous one, and the last chunk ends at the last word. Raise ValueError unless 0 <= overlap < size. On a 40-word text with size=12, print the chunk count and starting words for overlap 0, 4, and 8. Before you run it, predict the three counts with ceil((n − overlap) / (size − overlap)).

Need a hint?

Move a start index forward by size - overlap each time. Stop right after appending a chunk whose end, start + size, reaches or passes the number of words. Without the overlap < size check, a step of zero would loop forever.

Show solution

Overlap 8 doubles the chunk count compared with overlap 0. That means twice the index and twice the embedding cost, and a top-3 retrieval that often returns three nearly identical chunks. A small overlap, one sentence or a few words, gets the boundary benefit without the duplicates.

#Exercise 6: Measure retrieval with hit@k

Before judging answers, check that the retriever finds the right chunk. For each question below, rank the chunks by TF-IDF similarity (TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english")), find the gold chunk's rank, and report hit@1 and hit@3: the fraction of questions whose gold chunk is ranked first, or in the top 3.

Need a hint?

cosine_similarity(vectorizer.transform([question]), matrix)[0] gives one score per chunk. np.argsort(-scores, kind="stable") sorts best-first, and .index(gold) + 1 turns the position into a rank.

Show solution

Read the misses, not just the averages. The bags question loses to the plastic chunk, which says "plastic" twice and shares "bin". The cart question ranks the right chunk sixth of eight: "cart" matches the compost chunk exactly, while the pickup chunk says "Carts", and plain TF-IDF treats those as different words. The stemming analyzer from the build-along, or embeddings, would fix that. A retriever that misses one question in six puts a ceiling on every answer built on top of it.

#Challenge: Instructions hiding in a document

Retrieved text is data, but a model reads it with the same attention it gives your instructions. A chunk can contain an attack, called prompt injection. Write injection_flags(text) that returns which of a few regular-expression patterns match (ignore-previous-instructions phrasing, "you are now", mentions of the system prompt, and anything that looks like a <source> tag), and wrap_source(sid, text) that escapes &, <, and > so a document can't close its own source tag early. Run both on the three chunks below and explain what the patterns miss.

Need a hint?

Use re.search(pattern, text, re.IGNORECASE) for each pattern. For escaping, replace & first; otherwise you'd double-escape the & in <.

Show solution

S2 trips two patterns, and escaping turns its fake </source> into harmless text, so it can't pretend to end the source and start a new one. S3 trips nothing: it's a plain sentence with no magic words, and a pattern list will never cover every phrasing. Treat filters as a smoke alarm, not a lock. The defenses that hold up are structural: keep instructions in the system message, never let model output trigger actions without checks, validate every reply against a schema, and verify that answers are supported by sources, which is where Module 7 picks up.
